title: ‘Hershey’ Review: Finn Wittrock Plays the American Chocolate Titan in a Sickly Sweet Biopic
full_text: × Continue to The Hollywood Reporter SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All November 17, 2026 10:18am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Finn Wittrock (left) and Alexandra Daddario in 'Hershey.' Angel Studios The new film about the founder of the Hershey Company begins with a loving, beautifully lit close-up of one of the company’s signature products, a Hershey’s Kiss. That tells you pretty much everything you need to know about this effort produced in part by Hershey Entities and distributed by Angel Studios . Starring Finn Wittrock ( American Horror Story ) in the title role, Hershey is a blandly sanitized biopic that’s as sickly sweet as the candies the company sells. Being released for Thanksgiving, it essentially serves as a feature-length product placement. The film, which an opening title card informs us is “based on the unlikely true story,” begins in 1870 with a young Milton (James Kelly) growing up in a Mennonite community in rural Pennsylvania. After the tragic death of his younger sister and the abandonment of the family by his dreamer father ( Alan Ruck ), he begins working for a kindly confectioner, Joseph Royer ( Richard Kind , at his most twinkly), who teaches him candy-making methods. Related Stories TV AMC's 'Mayfair Witches: Salem Coven' Gets December Debut as Catherine Zeta-Jones, Carrie-Anne Moss Tease 'Kill Jackie' and 'Yaga' at NYCC TV Angel Studios' 'Homestead: The Series' Sets Season 2 Premiere Date and Cast (Exclusive) Hershey The Bottom Line Will give you cavities. Release date : Wednesday, November 25 Cast : Finn Wittrock, Alexandra Daddario, Alan Ruck, Richard Kind, David Costabile, James Kelly, Michael Moreland Milligan, Daniel David Stewart, Joel Brady, Francesca Faridany, Dina Spybey-Waters, John Hans Tester, Heléne Yorke, Mark Ashworth, Isabel Van Natta Director : Mark Waters Screenwriters : Sharon Paul, Timothy Michael Hayes Rated PG, 1 hour 50 minutes Milton is soon inventing original candies and eventually opens his own shop specializing in (oh, the irony) caramels. The shop fails but the young entrepreneur is undeterred, and he tries again with a store in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, that takes off after a bulk order from a visiting Englishman. The episodic screenplay by Sharon Paul and Timothy Michael Hayes chronicles Hershey’s rise to prominence in dutiful fashion, including his eventual transition to producing chocolates. This comes about after a visit from a salesman representing a German chocolate company, who, after being rejected by Hershey because the product tastes bitter, warns him, “I think you’re missing out on what’s next.” Sure enough, Hershey changes his mind, realizing that all the chocolate needs is some milk to make it taste better. The rest, as they say, is history. “Caramels are a fad, but chocolate is permanent,” Hershey confidently tells his associates. On his way to becoming a chocolate titan, Hershey meets the adorable Kitty ( Alexandra Daddario ), with their love story fueling much of the film’s second half. He turns the village where he grew up into the company town that still bears his name, treating his employees benevolently (the violent labor disputes that occurred in later years are ignored) and, at the urging of his wife, opening a school for impoverished youth that still exists today. (Left unmentioned is the fact that admission was restricted to whites; Black students weren’t admitted until 1968.) Another major plot element is Kitty’s serious illness, which prevents her from having children and results in numerous scenes that find her nearly collapsing while Milton looks on concernedly. Flavorlessly directed by Mark Waters (far past his Freaky Friday and Mean Girls glory days), Hershey never succeeds in coming to life, playing like the sort of candy-coated dramatized film that would find its most receptive audiences at the Hershey Story Museum in Pennsylvania. Every scene plays out exactly as you’d expect, with conflicts resolved serendipitously and Hershey benefiting from fortunate strokes of luck, including a malfunctioning machine producing what became the Hershey’s Kiss and the couple miraculously avoiding a planned voyage on the Titanic (they dance to their good fortune, which, considering what happened to the poor souls onboard, seems a bit tacky). Wittrock, eventually outfitted with a period-perfect moustache, does a reasonably good job but is ultimately unable to overcome the script’s deficiencies. Daddario fares better, conveying a tender warmth and playfulness that infuse the film with much of its heart. (Strangely, Wittrock eventually receives old age makeup treatment while Daddario looks virtually the same throughout). The supporting players, including David Costabile ( Billions ) as a composite business competitor, do exactly what’s expected of them. The film ends in predictable fashion, with vintage photographs of the real-life figures and present-day footage of the school and its grateful students. That’s followed by one of those annoying “Pay It Forward” pitches, gamely delivered by Wittrock and Daddario, urging us to pour more money into the studio’s coffers under the guise of philanthropy. title: Jena Malone, Suzanna Son & Sofia Mortera Wrap On Indie ‘Kismet’ From Giovanna Molina
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt Mentalist Oz Pearlman Sets December Release For First Netflix Special ‘Magic Of The Mind’ Larry David Sets Six-City Live Conversation Tour For February 2027 Comedian Nate Jackson Unveils Dates For 2027 Miracle Baby Tour View All November 17, 2026 10:13am Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Jena Malone, Suzanna Son, and Sofia Mortera Evan Mulling/Getty/Danielle Vernengo EXCLUSIVE: Jena Malone ( The Boroughs ) and Suzanna Son ( Monster: The Ed Gein Story ) have wrapped roles opposite newcomer Sofia Mortera in Kismet , an indie from Radiance Pictures and Distant Films that marks the feature debut of writer-director Giovanna Molina . Set during the desolate off-season on Fire Island, Kismet follows a melancholic 13-year-old girl (Mortera) who, in the wake of her parents’ separation, claims an alien has taken over her body to save her from her human emotions. Recently wrapping production, Kismet co-stars Elliot Villar and Riley Vinson, with Zuzanna Szadkowski, Matthew Sean Blumm, Marta Pozzan, Caitlin Hagney, David Staats and Lorena Ramos rounding out the cast. The film is produced by Molina, along with Zoey Pressey, Alexander Spenser Gould and Nuer Taqa. It’s cast by Betsy Fippinger, CSA. Related Stories News 'Hollow Moon': Sci-Fi With Jena Malone & Dermot Mulroney Gets Sales Deal & New Title News Jena Malone, Dermot Mulroney, Mekhi Phifer & Vannessa Vasquez Set A Mission As 'Moon People' Molina told Deadline, “It felt incredibly special to bring this talented cast and crew this fall to Fire Island, where I spent much of my childhood. Jena Malone is a coming-of-age sci-fi icon, so it’s truly full circle to have her supporting a young exciting newcomer like Sofia Mortera in a film that nods to DONNIE DARKO through a female lens. Throughout our shoot, the island took on a mythical shape that mirrored the uncanny nature of the film: beached whales, nor’easter floods, roaming deer, and a double rainbow, to name a few. Filming against this surreal backdrop was a remarkable experience.” Watch on Deadline A Golden Globe nominee, Malone has most recently been seen in the Netflix series The Boroughs , exec produced by The Duffer Brothers, as well as Jack Begert’s indie Junk , produced by Darren Aronofsky. Upcoming, she’ll be seen in the horror thriller Pendulum and Arkasha Stevenson’s untitled horror film for A24. She is represented by Entertainment 360, Gersh and Hirsch Wallerstein Hayum. Son is best known for her breakout turn opposite Simon Rex in Sean Baker’s Red Rocket , for which she was nominated for the Gotham Award for Breakout Performer as well as the Independent Spirit Award for Best Supporting Female. She recently appeared in Monster: The Ed Gein Story and will also be seen coming up in A24’s mystery film from Stevenson. She is repped by Curate, CAA and Jackoway Austen Tyerman. Mortera voices Young Priscilla in Netflix’s animated feature Steps and has appeared in the films Come Out and Play and The Spirit of Innocence . Additional voiceover credits include Netflix’s CoComelon Lane and Prime Video’s Agent Zeta . She is repped by DDO Artists Agency and Mills Kaplan Entertainment. A Mexican-Italian-American filmmaker from Brooklyn, NY, Molina’s work explores stories of isolation, belief and surrealism within a female coming-of-age context. She has received grants and fellowships from Sundance, PBS, The Future of Film is Female and the Saul Zaentz Innovation Fund. Her film Quaker had its world premiere at the 75th Berlin Film Festival and won Best Narrative Short at Bend Film Festival. She holds an MFA in Directing from the UCLA School of Theater, Film and Television and a BA from Johns Hopkins University, with degrees in The Writing Seminars and Film & Media Studies. She is represented by Circle Management + Production. title: ‘Heated Rivalry’ Star Connor Storrie, ‘Obsession’ Ingenue Inde Navarette and ‘Backrooms’ Filmmaker Kane Parsons Set as BAFTA U.S. Breakouts
full_text: × Continue to The Hollywood Reporter SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All November 17, 2026 10:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Connor Storrie Inde Navarrette Adam Meeks Kane Parsons and Stephanie Ahn. Getty Images (5) BAFTA has blessed its breakthrough class of 2026. The organization has revealed the roster of talent — actors and directors to writers and below-the-line standouts — selected to shine as its BAFTA Breakthrough U.S. cohort for the year. It’s a list of 14 “rising creatives” paving their way through film, television and games and “helping shape the future of the screen industries.” The list (in alphabetical order by first names with mention of their breakout project) includes Union County filmmaker Adam Meeks, The Burbs creator Celeste Hughey, Heated Rivalry heartthrob Connor Storrie , Nuisance Bear documentary director Gabriela Osio Vanden, 1923 and Frisco King costume designer Gaby Acosta, Night Nurse filmmaker Georgia Bernstein, Obsession star Inde Navarrette , Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 game lead writer and voice and localization producer Jennifer Svedberg-Yen, Despelote game lead developer Julián Cordero, Backrooms filmmaker Kane Parsons , Bandi composer Marcus Norris, Barbara Forever documentary editor Matt Hixon, Bedford Park filmmaker Stephanie Ahn and South Midnight game writer Zaire Lanier. Related Stories TV LGBTQ Representation on TV Dropped in 2025-26, GLAAD Study Finds Movies 'Wet,' Starring Connor Storrie, Rebecca Ferguson and Odessa A'zion, Acquired by Lionsgate Left to right: Matt Hixon, Marcus Norris, Adam Meeks, Zaire Lanier, Jennifer Svedberg-Yen, Kane Parsons, Gaby Acosta, Georgia Bernstein, Gabriela Osio Vanden and Julian Cordero. Credit: BAFTA/Lee Jameson BAFTA Breakthrough, supported by Apple TV, is now in its seventh year. It’s described as the arts charity’s flagship talent initiative, and is designed to support creatives at a pivotal point in their careers. The cohort receives access to professional development, industry connections and opportunities to build their networks within the creative community. They take part in a year-long program, which features one-on-one meetings and career guidance, full BAFTA voting membership, access to BAFTA events and screenings and networking opportunities here and abroad. “This year’s cohort reflects the imagination, ambition and distinct perspectives that continue to push our industries forward. At a time when emerging creatives face increasing challenges in finding opportunity, mentorship and a path forward, BAFTA is proud to create a space where talent can be recognized, supported and connected to a broader creative community,” explained BAFTA North America executive director Courtney LaBarge Bell. “Each member of this cohort brings a unique point of view and a commitment to their craft that we believe deserves to be seen and championed. Over the next year, we look forward to supporting their growth, creating meaningful connections and helping open doors as they continue to build lasting careers.” The roster was selected by a jury that included Adolpho Veloso, Alysa Nahmias, Arseni Khachaturan, Julia Kim, Peter Teschner, Rolfe Kent, Sonia Kennebeck, Bella Gonzales and Nana Mensah for film and TV, and Bethany Higa, Bhamini Lakshminarayan, Del Walker, Mai Koythong, Michael Surya, Nick Apostolides, Robert Dominguez and Virginia Leo for games. Alums include Stephanie Economou, HIKARI, Nava Mau, Bao Nguyen, Fernando Reyes Medina, Karrie Shirou Shao, Erica Tremblay, Cheyenne Pualani Morrin, Sean Wang, Erika Ishii, Eva Victor and Chase Infiniti. title: “In a Very Primal Way It’s About Who We Are as Queer Men in Our 60s”: ‘THR Presents’ Q&A With ‘Tip Toe’ Star Alan Cumming and Creator Russell T Davies
full_text: Continue to The Hollywood Reporter SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Seija Rankin Plus Icon Seija Rankin Senior Editor seijawrites Follow Sign Up View All November 17, 2026 10:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source “The idea rose up in me unstoppably,” says Russell T Davies of his new series Tip Toe . The creator, who was first put on the television map with his groundbreaking 1999 series Queer as Folk , had been working on another project when he found himself so increasingly alarmed by the state of the world and the cacophony of conservative and bigoted voices on the internet that he rushed home to Manchester to start writing a new script. “I’m well known as a gay writer and activist, and when you are that person in this modern world you automatically get called a pervert online,” he explained during a recent THR Presents panel. “I get called a pedophile and a groomer daily, you can just search for my name and there it is. I’m always thinking about terrible things that might happen to me every single day.” Related Stories TV 'The Traitors' Star Ben McDonnell on 'New Blood' Set Secrets and Alan Cumming: "You Can Never Break Character" Movies 'THR Presents' Q&A With Hana Jusic, Director of Croatian Oscar Contender 'God Will Not Help' That real-life horror became the story of Tip Toe , which follows opens with the violent hanging death of a queer bar owner at the hands of his conservative next-door neighbor and then jumps back in time to trace the seeds of the tragedy. The bar owner is played by Alan Cumming , who Davies refers to as a “sleeping giant.” Though Cumming has become known more recently for his bubbly hosting gigs on the Traitors franchise, Davies felt strongly that the actor had more to show audiences. The two first met over 20 years ago on a business lunch and have been trying to work together ever since. “I said yes as soon as he told me about the story,” says Cumming. “I feel like it’s a fateful thing that [our working together] happened in this way, with a show that means so much to both of us. In a very primal way it’s about who we are as queer men in our 60s.” Davies created the show with the UK’s Channel Four, and while he was ferociously writing the scripts he says he “warned” the network that they were coming. “When I eventually handed the script in to them, they commissioned the show within seven days. Nothing happens that fast. But seven days later in the middle of their Christmas dinner they said yes — that’s how much they felt it was important.” Watch the rest of the conversation between Cumming and Davies in the video above. title: Why Denis Villeneuve Cast Robert Pattinson as James Bond: ‘I Need to Believe This Man Is a Killer’
full_text: × Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Nov 17, 2026 9:51am PT Why Denis Villeneuve Cast Robert Pattinson as James Bond: ‘I Need to Believe This Man Is a Killer’ By Zack Sharf Plus Icon Zack Sharf Digital News Director ZSharf Latest Why Denis Villeneuve Cast Robert Pattinson as James Bond: ‘I Need to Believe This Man Is a Killer’ 29 minutes ago ‘Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Brad Pitt’s Sequel Is an ‘Absolute Triumph’ and a ‘Wildly Entertaining’ ‘Love Letter’ to Hollywood 12 hours ago Jennifer Lawrence Reunites With ‘Hunger Games’ Co-Star Josh Hutcherson at ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ World Premiere 18 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michael Buckner / Lia Toby Denis Villeneuve sat down for an interview with GQ magazine in the days before Robert Pattinson was officially announced as the new James Bond and broke down the most important qualities he was looking for in the search for his 007. The “Dune” and “Blade Runner 2049” director is helming Bond 26 at Amazon MGM Studios. “At the end of the day, the truth is, no matter who I choose, some people will be excited and others will be disappointed,” Villeneuve said about the search for his Bond actor, which reportedly included the likes of Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Nicholas Hoult and Jack Lowden before the director’s “Dune: Part Three” star Pattinson won the part. Related Stories NBCUniversal Invests in Black Vertical Drama Platform From 'Girls Trip' Producer Will Packer Jon Stewart Weighs In on Robert Pattinson’s James Bond Casting: ‘You Already Got Batman’ So what gave Pattinson the edge over his fellow Bond audition-mates? “The first quality is that I need to believe that this man is a killer, because more than a spy, Bond is an assassin,” Villeneuve said about what his Bond actor needed. “I need that kind of anger deep in the eye. It’s not everybody who has that.” “I need someone who has that kind of unapologetic panache, someone that when he comes into the room, everything starts to gravitate around him, that kind of strong charisma and someone that has a lot of sensuality as well and that people are attracted to… someone who has dark humor, someone that has pleasure in being in deep shit, someone who is not afraid to put his hand in the mud,” the director continued. “I need someone that is strong, muscular, someone that is a force. And someone, of course, who has a deep intelligence in the eyes, someone that is always ahead of us.” Pattinson clearly checked off all the above boxes to become Villeneuve’s Bond. The director issued a statement upon the news of Pattinson’s official casting in which he expressed “deep gratitude the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey.” “We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007,” Villeneuve added. “I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.” Pattinson shared in his own statement: “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime… To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.” Villeneuve and Pattinson will begin filming Bond 26 sometime in 2027. After Endgame is a lesson in both life and chess from someone who has taught over 6,500 chess lessons. Doyle takes the audience on a journey across the globe as he is flown to the vibrant city of Singapore at the behest of a mysterious investor. There, he finds himself imparting chess wisdom to some of the world’s wealthiest individuals. Tensions rise as he navigates these high-stakes players, both on and off the chessboard. The partnership will introduce the Miss Dior x Women at Sundance Institute Award, honoring an emerging filmmaker whose work is making an impact on the industry. Natalie Portman , the longtime face of Miss Dior, will present the inaugural award at the festival, which will take place Jan. 21-31 in Boulder, Colo., marking its first edition since relocating from Park City, Utah. The partnership also includes the Women at Sundance Institute Miss Dior Momentum Fellowship, which will support six women filmmakers developing their second or third feature films. The year-round program will provide non-recoupable grants, mentorship, professional development opportunities, industry networking and access to Sundance Institute’s educational programs and alumni network. Both initiatives will be celebrated at the Women’s Celebration Brunch Presented by Dior during the 2027 festival, where Portman will present the inaugural award. “For me, Miss Dior has always represented the courage to embrace your own voice with optimism, independence, and conviction,” Portman said in a statement. “I’m proud to see this spirit come to life through the partnership with Sundance Institute, celebrating women whose creativity will continue to inspire future generations.” The collaboration is the latest example of luxury fashion houses expanding their influence in Hollywood, increasingly investing in filmmaker development, production and festival programming. Chanel has maintained a two-decade relationship with the Tribeca Festival, including its Through Her Lens women’s filmmaker program, which celebrated its 11th edition in September. Cartier has partnered with the Venice Film Festival since 2021, while Miu Miu has commissioned short films by women directors through its “Women’s Tales” series since 2011, regularly presenting new installments at Venice. The Dior partnership also builds on Sundance Institute’s existing efforts to support women in film. Established in 2012, Women at Sundance Institute expanded its fellowship programming in 2018 with the Momentum Fellowship, designed to support filmmakers at pivotal stages of their careers. “We’re proud to partner with Dior in championing women artists whose bold, original stories deepen our understanding of the human experience and shape the future of independent storytelling,” said Michelle Satter, Sundance Institute’s founding senior director of artist programs. Revenue for fiscal 2026 hit $6.1 billion and revenue and delivered more than $110M of pro forma adjusted EBITDA, exceeding guidance. On a quarterly basis, revenue ticked up to $1.5 billion from $1.1 billion in the year-ago period, with net losses per share coming in at 44 cents. The company ended fiscal 2026 with 5.75 million subscribers, down from 6 million in the year-earlier period. Related Stories News Disney Breaks Down $3 Billion In Planned Cost Savings News TikTok Creator Videos Coming To Disney+ In December As Hulu Integration Takes Full Effect The results were reported on a pro-forma basis to reflect the timing of Disney’s acquisition of a 70% stake in Fubo, which it has combined with Hulu + Live TV. Watch on Deadline Shares in Fubo climbed 11% on the news as of mid-day, on above-average trading volume, reaching $8.20. The Disney-Fubo transaction closed in October 2025, finalizing a months-long resolution of a landmark antitrust lawsuit. Fubo, which launched as a sports-focused pay-TV service in 2025, sued Disney, Fox and Warner Bros. Discovery over the media giants’ plan to launch subscription streaming outlet Venu Sports. The complaint alleged antitrust violations and a judge sided with Fubo’s argument that programmers had engaged in monopolistic behavior. Alisa Bowen, a longtime Disney streaming executive who was installed as CEO earlier this year , said the relationship with her former company gives Fubo advantages in the areas of cost synergies, ad sales and marketing. “Leveraging Disney’s broad reach is one of the efficient ways to build brand awareness and to reach potential new subscribers,” Bowen told Wall Street analysts during Fubo’s quarterly earnings call. (While the company remains a separate publicly traded entity, its financial reporting lines up with that of Disney, which reported strong quarterly numbers in parallel with Fubo.) The company has already begun adding Disney+ and Hulu as free add-ons for Fubo subscribers, with additional benefits ahead in December when Hulu + Live TV is added to Disney+ as part of a long-developing integration plan . In her quarterly letter to shareholders, Bowen noted the completion of a strategic review, which determined that Fubo should focus on three key initiatives. Those include leaning into its heritage as a sports-focused operator; exploring new content and experiences, especially in mobile; and increasing efficiency in pursuit of profitability. Ad revenue in the quarter jumped 22% to $119.1 million. “We continued to benefit from a significant lift in CPMs and fill rates, including as a result of the integration of Fubo ad inventory on the Disney Advertising Server,” Bowen wrote in the shareholder letter. title: ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Dune 3,’ ‘Michael’ and More Top Artisans Honored at Hamilton Behind the Camera Awards
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Nov 17, 2026 9:30am PT ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Dune 3,’ ‘Michael’ and More Top Artisans Honored at Hamilton Behind the Camera Awards By Tanya Fedak Plus Icon Tanya Fedak Latest CAA and Hybe Launch Strategic Partnership 17 hours ago Jesse Eisenberg, Gina Prince-Bythewood, Beth de Araújo and Dawn Porter to Be Honored at Sundance Fundraiser Event 4 days ago Top Limited Series Writers on the Importance of Episode Titles and Adapting Well-Known Films and True Stories: ‘You Come Out With Something Familiar and Surprising’ 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Cinema’s top artisans were honored at the 15th Annual Hamilton Behind the Camera Awards in partnership with Variety on Friday, celebrating the artists whose behind-the-scenes contributions brought some of the world’s biggest films to life. Hosted by actor and comedian Asif Ali, this year’s honorees included the creative teams behind “ The Odyssey ,” “Dune: Part Three,” “The Invite,” “ Michael ,” “Club Kid,” “La Bola Negra,” “Paper Tiger,” “Wicker,” “The Debut” and “Wild Horse Nine.” Related Stories The Game Awards Nominations 2026: 'GTA 6' Lands Game of the Year Nom Ahead of Thursday Release Music Industry Moves: Felipe Holguin Named CEO of Universal Music Latin America and Iberian Peninsula “Dune” director Denis Villeneuve presented the cinematography award to Linus Sandgren, crediting the cinematographer with helping him reimagine the franchise and convincing him to shoot the third installment using an Imax film camera. “His versatility as a cinematographer is absolutely outstanding. More importantly, Linus is a poet, a very special soul,” Villeneuve said in his introduction. “He is a free spirit and one of the most beautiful humans I have ever met. His joy for filmmaking and passion for cinema are incredibly contagious.” In his acceptance speech, Sandgren revealed that he and the creative team partnered with Atlas Lens to develop custom, large-format Imax lenses to help bring a new vision of Arrakis to life. By the time production wrapped, the team had shot on “every single format, from Imax 65mm film to digital to poetic 16mm,” as well as black and white film. “Every format is carefully chosen for the emotions that Denis wanted to evoke in each shot,” Sandgren told the audience. “He challenged us to be inventive.” Also honored were Willie Burton, Craig Henighan, Gary A. Rizzo and Kevin O’Connell, the sound team behind “The Odyssey.” Matt Damon introduced the sound award, recalling that nearly all the sounds in the film were organic and that he never had to loop a single line of dialogue in post-production. “There’s many people with us behind the scenes: Foley artists, dialogue editors, sound effects editors, assistance, re-recording mixers or re-recording texts,” Henighan said. “I just want to thank and give a shoutout to all of them. Everyone behind the scenes really contributed to everything that we did, and we could bring our best.” The costume design award went to Marci Rodgers for her work on “Michael,” which was introduced by Jaafar Jackson. As a longtime fan of the musician, Rodgers recalled studying Michael Jackson’s artistry from a young age and dreaming of one day designing his costumes. “As artists, we all know what it means to carry a dream. Michael and I alike must speak it into existence and turn belief into action,” Rodgers said. “But believing in that dream also means you have to have the courage to pursue it. So don’t give up on your dream, even when it becomes heavy.” Tracee Ellis Ross presented the screenwriting award to Rashida Jones and Will McCormack for “The Invite,” joking that the honorees previously dated for only a few weeks. The duo, who have been writing together for nearly 20 years, said they are often drawn to using comedy to ground stories of heartbreak. “We have found some really hard moments in our lives have also been the funniest, and that’s really what drew us to ‘The Invite’: These four people in one apartment trying desperately to hold on to love and the people they dreamed they would be, even as their lives they built begin to fall apart,” Jones said. “Because sometimes, the only way through heartbreak is to laugh, and sometimes laughter is what makes it possible to tell the truth.” Diego Quecano received the property master award for “Club Kid,” presented by Jordan Firstman. One of the biggest challenges Quecano faced was recreating the textures of the drugs used in the film, particularly 3-MMC, which he ultimately replicated by mixing lactose powder with vitamin D and heating it up in the oven. “The textures of all the drugs had to be perfect,” Firstman told Variety ‘s senior entertainment writer Angelique Jackson on the red carpet. “3-MMC has a very different texture than K and coke. K is saltier, and coke is more powdery.” When asked about the queer representation among the cast and crew of “Club Kid,” Quecano told Variety that he hopes the industry continues to “see us. That we’re there, and we know how to do it. And just trust us, because sometimes we have to prove to them once, twice and three times that we are able to do it.” Alexander Skarsgård presented the hair and makeup award to Joe Dunckley for “Wicker” which required transforming the actor into a wooden man through an extensive prosthetics process. During his introduction, Skarsgård jokingly thanked Dunckley for allowing his lifelong dream of being made of wicker come true. “At Wētā Workshop, we combine the art form of weaving with new methods of directly 3D printing prosthetic makeup, creating a weave that moved with Alexander’s performance,” Dunckley said. “That innovation came from collaboration. 80 people at Wētā Workshop contributed to this character. I’m proud of what we achieved together.” Anne Ross received the production design award for “The Debut,” which was presented to her by the film’s creator, Jesse Eisenberg. He recalled first working with Ross on the 2005 “The Squid and the Whale,” where she asked everyone on set to bring in books to help fill the background of a scene. “When I was making this new movie, ‘The Debut,’ I wanted someone who would be able to go bigger in scope than the budget we had, and I thought I needed the person who collected those books,” Eisenberg said. “I needed someone who would ask the cast and crew for books instead of just settling for a smaller bookshelf, and that is Anne. The way I think about working with Anne is that she is good at every single thing that I am not good at, and I trust her completely.” John Malkovich presented the directing accolade to Martin McDonagh for “Wild Horse Nine,” recalling that he had previously turned down the filmmaker’s offers to star in “A Behanding in Spokane” and “Seven Psychopaths” before finally accepting his latest film. “By this point in the relationship, most people would take the hint,” Malkovich joked in his introduction. “But Martin is a man who once wrote a character who cut off his own fingers just to prove a point. So thank God I didn’t have a scheduling conflict when he asked me to be in ‘Wild Horse Nine.’” During his acceptance speech, McDonagh praised Malkovich’s “astonishing performance,” citing it as “the main reason I’m up here tonight.” He also told Variety that he would “love to be a small part” of helping the actor win his first Oscar. “To watch him go up there and get it would be kind of cool! I’d be like a giddy kid,” McDonagh said on the red carpet. Scott Morris took home the editing prize for “Paper Tiger,” which was presented by Miles Teller. In editing the James Gray film, Morris said he prioritized the characters, letting their mood guide the story. “The cutting room is very much a place of trust and creative freedom. Together, we’re working toward this common goal,” Morris said in his acceptance speech. “It’s this beautiful corroboration where we’re on this journey of exploration. I’m so grateful that James [Gray] brought me into his world.” The final award of the night was presented to Raül Refree by Judeline for the score of “La Bola Negra.” “Raül gave the Spanish classic ‘Soldadito Español’ a completely new meaning, moving away from its epic spirit to reveal something much more intimate: the sadness and loneliness of war,” Judeline said in her introduction. “Not just one war, but any war… His music doesn’t just accompany the images. It tells its own story.” Refree revealed he and directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi — commonly known as Los Javis — discussed creating “La Bola Negra” for years, and the filmmakers asked him to “compose some music” in advance that they could use for inspiration while writing the script. “Los Javis, they are very clever, and they give you all the space that you need to try to tell your own vision of the story,” Refree told Variety on the red carpet. “That made me feel super free to compose.” The composer also teased that Calvo and Ambrossi already “have an idea” for their next project, and he trusts “they are going to make an incredible step forward.” James Bond Final Screen Tests Are Happening This Week Robert Pattinson’s 007 Announcement on Social Media Proves Amazon Is Already Changing the Bond Franchise ‘Triplets of Belleville’ Director Sylvain Chomet Fires Back at AI Accusations Over Dior Film Featuring Robert Pattinson’s Voice: ‘Everything Was Drawn by Hand’ (EXCLUSIVE) Inside Omega’s James Bond Exhibition, From 007’s Toothbrush to His Passport and Mini Car Bombs Ben Affleck Raved About Robert Pattinson’s ‘The Odyssey’ Performance, Recalls Matt Damon: He Said ‘It Was Like Watching a Guy Run Into an Avalanche’ Critics Vindicate ‘Artificial’ After Messy Amazon MGM Breakup (and the Studios vs. Talent Wars Around AI Are Just Beginning) Loading comments...

All of this comes before Paramount’s release of Warner Bros/Legendary’s expected mega holiday tentpole Dune: Part Three, for which Goldstein plotted the distribution attack plan that includes 70MM Imax ticket sellouts (a similar situation to Universal’s The Odyssey in its pre-opening). Viane and Barber report into Goldstine. Where to begin on Goldstein’s long list of accomplishments? He handled distribution during his career on more than 1,000 Warner Bros movies. Goldstein was raised to Head of Global Distribution early last year in what turned out to be a milestone year for Warners, with $4.3 billion at the global box office off such hits as A Minecraft Movie, Weapons, Final Destination: Bloodlines, Superman as well as multi Oscar winners One Battle After Another and Sinners. Goldstein was heavily involved in the releases of the Harry Potter and Dark Knight franchises, and Zack Synder DC movies as EVP when Dan Fellman was the president of domestic distribution. More importantly, he was a champion in getting cinemas reopened post-Covid for the theatrical release of Christopher Nolan’s Tenet (a pretty good feat sans the bulk of the L.A. market and NYC). Following that, Goldstein had to manage and make the best of Jason Kilar’s controversial theatrical day-and-date strategy during the remainder of Covid, beginning with 2020’s Wonder Woman 1984 and ending with 2021’s The Matrix Resurrections. Despite that Covid slate opening in theaters and premiering on HBO Max at the same time, Goldstein was able to squeeze out some hits out specifically Legendary’s Dune ($410.7M WW) and Godzilla vs. Kong ($470M WW), both titles’ sequels seeing bigger grosses at the box office in their pure theatrical runs (read Dune Part Two’ s $714.8M WW and Godzilla x Kong ‘s $572M WW. Goldstein joined Warners in 1978 as a sales trainee in the Los Angeles office before relocating to the company’s regional offices in Florida, Ohio and Massachusetts (anecdotally, I’ve enjoyed hearing his stories about his dealings with my hometown movie cinema the Latchis Theatre in Brattleboro, VT). Goldstein became branch manager of the Boston office in 1980 and returned to L.A. in 1987 as a Western division sales manager. A year later, he was promoted to VP and Western division manager. In 1996, he was raised to SVP domestic distribution. In 1998, he became SVP and assistant general sales manager. In April 1999, he became SVP and general sales manager, before becoming EVP and general sales manager under Domestic Distribution president Fellman. After Fellman retired as president in December 2015 after a 37-year run at Warners, Goldstein was promoted to President of Domestic Distribution. Goldstein, a Syracuse University alum, will be missed for his premiere and event flashy suits — including pink at Barbie and a shiny gold get-up at this year’s CinemaCon where he showed off Tom Cruise’s Digger. title: Skydance Film Re-Org: Kira Goldberg Joins Paramount, Jesse Ehrman Upped to Run Warner Bros.
full_text: × Continue to The Hollywood Reporter SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Mia Galuppo , Aaron Couch , Borys Kit November 17, 2026 9:11am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jesse Ehrman, Michael Ireland, Kira Goldberg and Don Granger Presley Ann Slack/Oscars/Getty Images; Earl Gibson III/Penske Media/Getty Images; Rodin Eckenroth/Oscars/Getty Images; Michael Tullberg/Getty Images Skydance is sorting out its film operations at both Paramount and Warner Bros. in the wake of closing its $111 billion acquisition of Warners. Kira Goldberg is leaving Netflix, where she was one of its top film heads, overseeing faith-based, family and young adult films for the streamer. At Paramount, she will oversee film operations with longtime Skydance executive and producer Don Granger as presidents of the motion picture group. Jesse Ehrman , a twenty-year veteran of Warners, has been elevated to president of the motion picture group at the studio. He most recently served as president of production and development. Mikey Ireland, who joined Warners in February after being laid off at Paramount, will remain as president of production at Warners. Warner Bros. has been without a head since Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy were fired last month amid the Skydance merger. The duo had run the studio since 2022, guiding it to a best picture win with One Battle After Another earlier this year and having celebrated hits like Sinners , A Minecraft Movie and Weapons , but seeing a number of their 2026 movies bomb at the box office, most recently the Tom Cruise feature Digger . Elsewhere in today’s announcement was the news that Jeff Goldstein, a 48-year veteran of Warner Bros. who currently serves as the head of global distribution, will be exiting the studio, taking on a consulting role. The execs at Warners and Paramount will all report up to Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg, who oversee all of film for Skydance. The new re-org was done with an eye toward accomplishing the 30-plus movie slate across the two studios and their various divisions, which include New Line and DC Studios, which recently ousted James Gunn and Peter Safran and will install Marvel alum Jeremy Latcham next month. In the September settlement with California Attorney General Rob Bonta and other state AGs that cleared the path for the Warner Bros. merger, Skydance agreed that the combined studios must release 30 films for two years and then 32 for the next three years. There are penalties if this threshold isn’t met. For every movie that Skydance falls short of, the studio must pay $30 million to health and pension funds, split among the guilds. Additionally, a judge can force it to sell or spin out Miramax. Read the full memo from Goldberg and Greenstein below. Team, The theatrical business is central to the company’s vision for the future of Skydance. We are home to more than a century of extraordinary storytelling, legendary films and an enduring impact on audiences and culture around the world. We have both an incredible legacy to build upon and an enormous opportunity ahead of us: to champion the world’s best filmmakers, invest in ambitious storytelling and deliver an unparalleled slate of films that captivate audiences everywhere. As we shape this next chapter for Skydance, we want to share the leadership structure for the film divisions that comprise the Skydance Motion Picture Group. We said it on day one: Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures are our cornerstone labels and will remain distinct. Both will continue to anchor our biggest commercial and filmmaker-driven projects, with our animation and specialty labels also remaining separate with their own creative mandates. Our leadership structure is designed to empower each studio and label with dedicated creative leadership, backed by an excellent corporate team that provides the expertise, resources and support to help them succeed. Together, we are building an organization with the creative ambition, resources and scale to deliver on our commitment of 30 films per year. Studios Business Leadership Our corporate team brings collective expertise across key operations that ultimately support our creative output. The team comprises Courtney Armstrong, Chief Operating Officer; Mark Badagliacca, Chief Financial Officer; Brooke Robertson, EVP, Head of Global Communications & Media Relations; and Talia Robinson, EVP, Human Resources. Josh Goldstine has been named President of Worldwide Marketing and Distribution. Shaun Barber and Mark Viane will continue to report to Josh and oversee domestic and international distribution for both Paramount and Warner Bros. Jeff Goldstein, who has worked on over 1,000 films over 48 years of an illustrious career, will retire and transition into a consulting role. Jeff is a stalwart of this industry, and as we align these two organizations, his counsel will be tremendous. Additionally, Josh Silverman, President, Global Products & Publishing, will transition to our group to lead Consumer Products and Publishing, which will add important connectivity between our stable of IP and a key revenue stream. Mark Kaufman, EVP & Chief Content Officer, Theatre Ventures, will now report to Josh, where he will continue overseeing an acclaimed portfolio, including the Tony-winning Broadway production of The Lost Boys. Separately, we want to let you know that Ted Lim will be departing the company. We thank him for his leadership and contributions as Chief Business Officer and wish him all the best. Creative Leadership Paramount Pictures Don Granger and Kira Goldberg will lead Paramount Pictures as Presidents, Motion Picture Group. Over the last year, Don has been a great partner as we’ve repositioned the studio, bringing in key talent relationships and nearly doubling output. As our slate continues to grow, so does our team, and we’re thrilled to welcome Kira. Most recently at Netflix, she oversaw a slate that included Don’t Look Up, starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence, and the upcoming Bad Day with Cameron Diaz and The Take starring Denzel Washington and Robert Pattinson. Before that, she worked on films including Bohemian Rhapsody, The Post and The Greatest Showman during her tenure at Fox. Together, Don and Kira will work hand in hand going forward. Warner Bros. Pictures Jesse Ehrman has been elevated to President, Motion Picture Group. With over 20 years at Warner Bros., Jesse has been instrumental in many of the studio’s biggest hits including recent movies like A Minecraft Movie and Sinners, and has built lasting relationships with the studio’s most important filmmakers. Michael Ireland will continue as President of Production, reporting to Jesse. Mike’s relationships across the industry, strong eye for material and leadership experience make him an integral part of the motion picture group. DC Studios As we recently announced, Jeremy Latcham is joining us as President and Chief Creative Officer of DC Studios. James Gunn and Peter Safran will step away from their leadership roles after four years transforming and resetting the studio’s foundation and return full time to their creative work. Animation As part of this restructuring, Bill Damaschke will exit Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, and has agreed to stay for a period of time until he transitions to full-time producing. We thank him for his dedication to the animation business and greatly respect his commitment to this craft. In the interim, Jennifer Dodge and Traci Balthazor will oversee all animation across both Paramount and Warner Bros. Pictures, while Chris Leahy will continue to oversee the day-to-day operations of Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, reporting into Jennifer and Traci. John Lasseter remains Head of Skydance Animation alongside Holly Edwards, President, Skydance Animation. Specialty Labels and Divisions Our specialty labels and divisions will be led by Richard Brener, President, Chief Content Officer, New Line; Lia Buman, EVP, Head of Global Acquisitions and Republic Pictures; J.D. Lifshitz and Raphael Margules, Heads of Paramount Primal; Christian Parkes, Head of Clockwork; and Charlie Tabesh, SVP and General Manager, Turner Classic Movies. This team brings deep knowledge of our businesses, strong creative instincts and longstanding relationships across the industry. We have tremendous confidence in these leaders and are grateful for their partnership. Our shared responsibility is to give our filmmakers, storytellers and teams the support they need to do their best work. As we continue to build out the broader organization, this leadership structure establishes a strong foundation for the work ahead. We know how much work is underway across the company, and we’re grateful for the care, focus and dedication you bring to it every day. We look forward to all that we will build and accomplish together. Dana & Josh THR

title: Another Day, Another Outage: As CNN Reports On NSA Network Down, News Outlets Seize On Back-To-Back Incidents Of Cyber Chaos
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Political Ad Spending On 2025-26 Cycle Topped $12 Billion, A Boon To Broadcasters, Streaming And Digital Donald Trump Rages At ‘60 Minutes’ Report On Lack Of U.S. Preparedness For Iran’s Drone Counterattacks Willie Geist To Depart MS NOW’s ‘Morning Joe,’ Will Expand NBC News Role And Continue To Host ‘Sunday Today’ View All November 17, 2026 9:10am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Passengers waiting during a nationwide groundstop on Friday. Photo by Ryan Murphy/Getty Images CNN reported on Tuesday that the classified communications network used by the National Security Agency was down, giving further fuel to a cable news headline trendline of cyber chaos. The latest outage follows the Microsoft Outlook outage on Thursday, followed by an FAA air traffic control system glitch that grounded flights nationwide for much of the late afternoon and evening on Friday. Then there was the disruption on Monday to online banking, and a United Airline system outage later in the day. “Tech troubles take a toll as U.S. outages pile up,” read the chyron on Fox News , which led its 11 a.m. ET hour with the past days of turmoil. Related Stories News Political Ad Spending On 2025-26 Cycle Topped $12 Billion, A Boon To Broadcasters, Streaming And Digital Legal OpenAI Slapped By California AG For "Unfair & Unsafe Practices"; Sam Altman-Run Tech Firm Accuses State Of Improperly Singling Out Company Citing unnamed sources, CNN reported that there was no evidence of a cyberattack in the case of the NSA outage. Watch on Deadline The FBI on Tuesday did issue a flash advisory warning that “cybercriminals and state-aligned hackers are exploiting ARTEX, a super intelligence-powered penetration testing framework, to automate attacks against businesses and organizations worldwide.” On the network on Monday, Brit Hume said, “When they mount up to this number over a short period of time like this, you have to be at least suspicious that this isn’t mischief from a foreign adversary or maybe from a domestic adverary of some kind. They always say, ”There’s no indication of terrorism or there’s no indication of enemy conduct here,’ but I think we ought to wait a while before we come to any final conclusions on that.” As commenters wondered if there was some kind of connection between the outages, the White House has been downplaying the reports. On his trip to Asia, Donald Trump told reporters, “It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen, it’s fine.” Also on Monday, the security platform Report URI reported that some 178 companies and organizations, including Zoom, the BBC, CNN and Peacock, were exposed to malicious JavaScript that exploited vulnerabilities in the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. Also impacted, per the report, were Salesforce, IKEA and Equifax, among others, but most of the code was removed by the end of the day. A spokesperson for Optimizely did not immediate respond to a request for comment. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) told reporters, “I think it’s time for the administration to come up to the Hill and explain themselves so we can be informed about the steps that need to be taken.” On CNN, Chris Krebs, former director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, was a bit circumspect when trying to connect the dots between the various outages. He said, “I think more than anything, what it shows is virtually every aspect of our lives are now digitally connected. We have so many things that rely on functioning connected digital services, and those underlying services, whether they’re provided by a large vendor or a small vendor, might be a little rickety. Might be based on two decades worth of technology, and in some cases, some technical debt that needs to be updated.” He added, “AI is adding a complexity here because we’re using AI to find vulnerabilities in softwares and systems, and we’re patching systems at a rate far beyond anything in the past. Even just the last six months alone, we’re finding vulnerabilities and patching at just an absolutely insane pace. And anytime you do a patch, anytime you roll an update, it can introduce it can destabilize the system.” Meanwhile, at 2:20 p.m. ET on Tuesday, TV viewers will be treated to a test of the emergency alert system, conducted across broadcasters, cable systems, satellite radio and wireline video providers, per the FCC. The timing may be disconcerting right on the heels of the outages, but it’s required by law at least once every three years. Viewers also will be fully warned: It’s a test, and it’s only a test. title: British Lawmakers To Probe Use Of NDAs In Entertainment Industry
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max Sharon Horgan Honored By Canneseries 2027 Cricket Legend Ben Stokes Launches Production Company ‘A Passage To India’: Ali Fazal, Fiona Shaw & Tom Mison Leading BBC & CBC’s TV Reboot View All November 17, 2026 9:07am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Russell Brand Getty Image British lawmakers are to probe the use of non-disclosure agreements ( NDAs ) in the entertainment industry. As its chair Caroline Dinenage writes to Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy following the Russell Brand , David Walliams and MAFS UK scandals, the influential Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee (DCMSC) said it will hold an evidence session examining whether NDAs are preventing people from reporting abusive and unacceptable behavior. Taking place on December 7, witnesses for the session will soon be revealed. Related Stories News BBC Deletes Russell Brand Prison Clip After Playing It "In Error" On 'Today' Show News Channel 4 Boss Says "We Cannot Apologize Enough" To Russell Brand Victim Whose Complaint Was Twice Not Dealt With By Broadcaster The topic is a hot-button one amid multiple scandals. Channel 4 boss Priya Dogra and chair Geoff Cooper appeared in front of the DCMSC earlier today and were questioned on the network’s use of NDAs, which the pair stressed are done in a limited way with “pretty large caveats.” Watch on Deadline One lawmaker referenced Deadline’s exclusive report from last year that found Channel 4 had paid out nearly £5M ($6.6M) to ex-employees who signed settlement deals to prevent complaints escalating, but in doing so, stipulated that they do not discuss matters relating to the company. At the time, Zelda Perkins, the former assistant to Harvey Weinstein who became a vocal critic of NDAs, accused Channel 4 of “playing legal God” in what it allows former employees to express about the broadcaster. The recent Employment Rights Act introduced restrictions on employers using NDAs to prevent workers speaking about workplace harassment or discrimination. Dogra and Cooper were also quizzed at length about the ex-Channel 4 employee who was sexually assaulted by Brand in 2009 and said her complaints were twice not dealt with by the broadcaster. Dogra said “we cannot apologize enough” to the woman and stressed that Channel 4 has uprooted its procedures since. Will government fund CIISA? Elsewhere, Dinenage penned a letter to UK Culture Sec Lisa Nandy, who held a summit yesterday with entertainment industry bosses on bad behavior, posing a number of questions including what action she will be taking on bad behavior and what the likely timetable will be. Dinenage, who asked for a response by December 2, quizzed Nandy on the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority (CIISA), the anonymous whistleblowing service that has just got up and running. She asked whether CIISA has the “authority, capacity and sustainable funding it needs to fulfil its role” and questioned whether the government should “provide a backstop for its funding.” Nandy has repeatedly backed CIISA and chided some entertainment industry companies for failing to fund the service. Next week, CIISA will for the first time unveil a list of its financial backers. Earlier, Dogra said indies who work with Channel 4 will now have to be mandatorily registered with CIISA. Dinenage’s questions to Nandy in full You have said that if, at the summit, you find that protections are insufficient, you will not hesitate to take further action. How satisfied were you with the assurances you received from industry leaders? Is further action still on the table, and, if so, what form might it take and what is the likely timetable? What consideration have you given to measures that would require companies and organisations across these sectors to engage with the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority beyond the minimum? What form could these measures take? What assessment have you made of whether CIISA has the authority, capacity and sustainable funding it needs to fulfil its role? Will you consider providing a backstop for its funding, so its continued operation is not solely dependent on voluntary industry participation? What assessment have you made of the mechanisms available across the media and wider creative industries to report abuse, harassment, bullying and other unacceptable behaviour? What steps can be taken to make these mechanisms consistent, transparent, trusted and easily accessible, including to freelancers, people on short-term contracts and junior employees? And what steps can be taken to require employers to monitor the effectiveness of their reporting procedures? To what extent do recent developments make the case for the confidential whistleblowing service recently launched by CIISA? What assessment have you made of the impact that repeated revelations about bullying, harassment and predatory behaviour have on the morale of those working in the sector, the reputation of our world leading creative industries, and the economic impact of workplace conflict and legal settlements? Are the lines of responsibility and accountability clear enough in cases where programmes are commissioned by broadcasters but made by independent production companies? To what extent should our publicly owned broadcasters, the BBC and Channel 4, take the lead in raising standards in this area? In your view, are they doing enough? You said at DCMS questions that you were working closely with colleagues at the Ministry of Justice about the use of non-disclosure agreements to stop victims of abusive behaviour speaking out. Please could you update us on these discussions? Have you had any discussions with the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade about the implementation of relevant provisions in the Employment Rights Act 2025? What further steps could the Government take to tackle the cynical use of NDAs and other legal mechanisms in such circumstances? title: Report Reveals How & When Climate Issues Appear In Film & TV Scripts
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart ‘Sintonia’ Creator KondZilla On His New Netflix Series ‘Grifters’: Watch Trailer Rola Bauer Takes On Creative Director Role At Monte-Carlo Festival As Talent Agents & Producers Join Advisory Board SAG-AFTRA Boss Says AI Takedowns Matter More Than Damages To Performers View All November 17, 2026 9:03am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Outer Banks' Netflix Climate change is showing up more in film and TV. A study measuring how often a batch of key climate-related words occurred in over 35,000 scripts from 2021 to 2024 found the keywords were present in 3.2% of cases. That was a 14% uptick on the previous measurement period across 2016 to 2020, but remains relatively small. The report hails from the USC Norman Lear Center and Good Energy , a not-for-profit climate change consultancy. The findings of the report for 2016 to 2020 led to film and TV being accused of ‘climate silence’. The latest picture shows an improvement, even if only by a modest margin. Related Stories News Film & TV Creatives Want More Climate Storytelling, But Face Barriers, Survey Finds Casting 'Landman': Colm Feore Among 4 Upped To Series Regular As Season 3 Starts Production The new report also measured occurrences of climate change wording with a broader selection of 105 keywords. Using that set of words and terms, almost 5,000 of the 35,000 scripts registered some climate wording. Watch on Deadline In the scripts with climate wording, the focus was more on individual behaviors, such as eating plant-based foods or driving an EV. A smaller proportion addressed systemic solutions such as renewable energy or carbon capture. Using the wider 105 word list, climate language was most common in medical drama, ahead of romance and comedy shows and films. Fossil fuel terms such as oil, coal, fracking, methane and offshore drilling appeared in only 1.1% of the 35,120 scripts reviewed. Landman , the Paramount+ drama about the Texas oil business, was, unsurprisingly given the plot, the outlier, with a script dense with fossil-fuel terminology. The report noted that climate was often invoked through specific story details, including “fracking” in Ghostbusters: Afterlife , “solar energy” in Despicable Me 4 , “reforestation” in Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania , and “biodiversity” in Outer Banks . Films, meanwhile, were more likely than TV episodes to include climate terms. Measuring the occurrence of climate language by platform saw Apple TV top of the pile, ahead of Prime Video and then Netflix. Among the U.S. broadcast nets, Fox ranked first, ahead of ABC. title: New Report Finds Climate Change Storytelling Is Up
full_text: × Continue to The Hollywood Reporter SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Kirsten Chuba Plus Icon Kirsten Chuba Events Editor kirstenchuba Follow Sign Up View All November 17, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Tom Cruise in 'Digger.' Courtesy of Warner Bros. The USC Norman Lear Center has teamed up with environmental group Good Energy for a deep dive on how Hollywood is addressing climate change . “The Evolution of Climate Onscreen” report, released on Tuesday, tracks how conversations around climate change show up in scripted entertainment. The study looked at 35,120 scripts between 2021 and 2024, an update to its last report that looked at film and TV between 2016 and 2020. (Therefore a major climate project like Digger , from earlier this year , was not included in the research window). Related Stories Lifestyle Joel Kim Booster to Host Jackson Wild and Hollywood Climate Summit Media Awards Movies Ben Affleck Warns 'Digger' Box Office Bomb Will Lead to "A Bunch of Sh***y Homogenized Movies" The new report finds that climate-related keywords appeared in 3.2 percent of all scripts between 2021-2024, a 14 percent increase from the 2016-2020 findings . Across 100 storylines where climate was prominent, 87 percent featured climate impacts like rising sea levels, bad air, food stress or biodiversity loss; 72 percent highlighted climate change through disasters, mostly floods, extreme heat and hurricanes or storms; and 66 percent portrayed causes of climate change such as plastics, industrial agriculture, deforestation or fossil fuels. Additionally, climate solutions appeared in 10 percent of storylines, and nearly three times as many highlighted individual consumer behaviors over clean energy or other large-scale solutions. Medical and romance were found as the top two genres for climate storytelling to appear. “Climate is becoming more visible in film and television, but counting references can only tell us so much. For the first time, we have a map of the stories themselves. Disasters dominate, but nearly two-thirds of the climate storylines we studied also include causes, now bringing the human choices and systems behind the crisis into view,” Good Energy founder and CEO Anna Jane Joyner said in a statement. “At their center are complicated people — what they love, what they stand to lose, how they respond individually and together, and the fear, grief, humor, courage and wonder that emerge along the way. What thrills me is the rich creative territory artists are already exploring, and all that still lies ahead as they examine what it means to be human in the age of climate change.” Added USC Norman Lear Center director of research Erica Rosenthal, “We were honored to re-team with Good Energy on this groundbreaking research. In addition to tracking an increase in discussions of climate change over the last several years, we did a deep-dive into the themes and context of 100 climate stories. We found nearly three in four portrayed or mentioned disasters, but over the course of these stories, the dominant tone shifted from threat toward human agency.” “This is the first study to look at both how often climate comes up in Hollywood’s scripts and how it’s actually portrayed on screen. While modest in volume, climate visibility is growing in depth and range,” said Good Energy head of narrative research and strategy Bruno Olmedo-Quiroga. “Across more than 35,000 scripts, the climate conversation came up in about one in seven, on every major network and streamer, in comedies, romances and even horror. Writers are already bringing climate into every kind of story. And we now know what they portray, the characters at their center, and how their emotional journeys unfold.” THR

title: ‘Madden’ Review: Nicolas Cage and Christian Bale Go for Broke in a Cartoonish Biopic From David O. Russell That’s Strictly for Football Fanatics
full_text: × Continue to The Hollywood Reporter SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All November 17, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source From left: Kathryn Hahn, Nicolas Cage, Christian Bale and Sienna Miller in 'Madden.' Quantrell Colbert/Prime Imagine being cornered at a party while sober by a wired cokehead determined to tell you a long, painstakingly detailed story without pausing for breath and you might have some idea of the exhausting experience of watching Madden . Full disclosure: I have almost no knowledge of or interest in football beyond religious devotion to all five seasons of Friday Night Lights . Which should in theory disqualify me from reviewing David O. Russell ’s feverish chronicle of John Madden’s career as legendary head coach for the Oakland Raiders and longtime NFL telecast commentator. But hey, the job’s the job. Related Stories Movies Robert Pattinson's Bondmaxxing: How 007 Still Has Pop Culture in a Vice Grip TV Fourth 'Terminal List' Show in the Works at Prime Video Even if I were passionate about pigskin, however, I can’t imagine getting much pleasure from this cartoonish biodrama, led by the kind of stunt acting from both principals that never lets you forget they are Giving a Performance. (Think Tom Cruise in Tropic Thunder . Or Digger .) This means that despite hurling themselves into their roles with gusto, there’s little to no risk of forming a human emotional connection with Nicolas Cage ’s Madden or Christian Bale ’s Al Davis, the longtime friend who was the Raiders’ owner and general manager. Madden The Bottom Line Should come with a concussion warning. Release date : Weds., Nov. 18 Cast : Nicolas Cage, Christian Bale, Kathryn Hahn, Sienna Miller, John Mulaney, Shane Gillis, Simms May, Luke Klein, Joel Murray, Mark Medrano Director : David O. Russell Screenwriter : David O. Russell, Cambron Clark Rated R, 1 hour 50 minutes Cage is encased in a fat suit so bulky he looks like a line drawing out of Family Guy , while Bale goes for a receding hairline, a mouth locked in a Harvey Keitel grimace and a chewy Brooklyn accent, matched by that of Sienna Miller as Davis’ wife Carol. Meanwhile, both Miller and Kathryn Hahn as Madden’s wife Virginia appear to have gone wig-shopping with Nicole Kidman. That’s a let-down coming from the director of one of the 21st century’s great hair movies, American Hustle . Co-written by Russell with Cambron Clark, Madden kicks off in 1976 when the Pro Football Hall of Famer’s days on the field are far behind him and he has racked up an impressive streak of winning seasons for the Raiders. But Super Bowl triumph remains elusive. That changes the following year when the team defeats the Minnesota Vikings to claim victory in Super Bowl IX. Virginia has bought John’s vague promises that he would take a breather once that milestone had been reached, finally spending more time with his wife and their sons Mike (Simms May) and Joe (Luke Klein) and maybe renewing their wedding vows. (He’s so consumed by his work that he can’t even remember the boys’ ages.) Having earned a pilot’s license, Virginia also hopes to coax John past his fear of flying and take him for a spin. But as Al keeps reminding him, football is who he is, so John stays on for another two seasons before a bleeding ulcer forces him into retirement. Connoisseurs of gonzo Cage performances might get a kick out of his characterization. The actor makes Madden a football visionary, with thousands of strategic plays in his head — or scrawled across the screen in noughts-and-crosses graphics. He’s a sports genius who can sometimes come across as borderline simple-minded, which adds to the innate sweetness Cage brings to the role. Even if he’s an absentee husband and dad much of the time, John’s love for his wife and sons is never in doubt. It’s just that they are in constant competition with his love for the game and his team. Even so, the conflict always feels low-stakes, even when the unaccustomed inactivity of retirement has John acting crazy, muttering football philosophy to the family’s dog. Unable to separate himself entirely from the game, he accepts an offer from CBS Sports to provide football commentary, his discursive, stream-of-consciousness patter ignoring the mandate to follow the lead of sportscaster Pat Summerall (Joel Murray), much to the latter’s frustration. But Russell skips right over any friction in their adjustment period, jumping ahead to the on-air bonhomie that made Madden and Summerall one of the most celebrated football commentary duos in sports broadcasting history. There’s an almost manic level of excitement from John as he scrawls complex plays onto a telestrator (like a not-hot version of Steve Kornacki on election nights), while Pat seems completely comfortable playing the amused straight man. The other significant thread starts with overtures from Trip Hawkins ( John Mulaney ), founder of video game company Electronic Arts, who masterminds what would go on to become a major success story with Madden NFL . John is skeptical at first, unimpressed with the clunky pixel figures Trip and his team of nerds demonstrate in an initial presentation of the sports game. But once John hands over the fat ring-binder file where he has recorded every play, the techies perfect the product, making it one of the top sellers in video game history. Al strenuously objects to John sharing his playbook, insisting that the contents are a vital part of his legacy with the Raiders that will ensure his place in “The Afterlife Football Hall of Fame.” But that recurring motif is about as substantial as the mockumentary setup that has Virginia addressing the camera from an armchair early on. Both wives are shortchanged by the script. Moments of drama like Virginia’s divorce threats or Carol’s stroke and subsequent period in a coma fizzle before they can gain much steam. Shane Gillis , the stand-up more famous for his racist, misogynistic and homophobic slurs than his comedy, appears as Madden’s idolizing next-door neighbor but brings very little to the table. The heart of the film, ostensibly, is the friendship between John and Al, but it’s hard to invest when the characters never feel much like real people. For anyone without an insatiable appetite for American football history, the story is seldom of much interest, which perhaps explains why three credited editors have cut the film at such a rollicking pace, and why Russell stuffs in period needle drops at every opportunity. Madden is an improvement on his last feature, the laborious 2022 screwball comedy Amsterdam . But like that movie it’s busy and abrasive, without being entertaining beyond the curiosity of Nicolas Cage bouncing around in a mound of prosthetics.
