Russell Screenwriter: David O. Russell, Cambron Clark Producers: Todd Black, Jason Blumenthal, Steve Tisch, Jonathan Shukat, David O. Russell, Matthew Budman, Colin Wilson Executive producers: David Bloomfield, Constance Scwartz-Morini, Michael Strahan Director of photography: Robert Richardson Production designers: David J. Bomba, Sean Ryan Jennings Costume designer: Madeline Weeks Music: Marcelo Zarvos Editors: Jon Poll, Alan Baumgarten, Mike Azevedo Sound designer: Ann Scibelli Visual effects supervisor: Allen Maris Casting: Mary Vernieu, Lindsay Graham Ahanonu Rated R, 1 hour 50 minutes THR

title: Billy Evans Fires Back at Amanda Seyfried and Nathan Fielder: “It’s My Life and I Love It”
full_text: × Continue to The Hollywood Reporter SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content Billy Evans and his dog Teddy Niki Boon The whole point of participating in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim ’s You Can See Everything , says Billy Evans , was to change the world’s perception of Elizabeth Holmes , the 42-year-old founder of Theranos currently serving out an 11-year sentence for defrauding investors. Their young children were already beginning to feel the repercussions when filming began, Evans says, being uninvited to playdates. But in the weeks since the film’s release, he finds himself facing a host of new problems, with strangers picking apart everything from the appearance of his genitals to how the couple makes scrambled eggs. Related Stories Movies Billy Evans Reacts to Amanda Seyfried's Portrayal of Elizabeth Holmes in 'You Can See Everything' Movies Johnny Depp's 'Ebenezer' Unwraps $19M to Win Weekend in Box Office Return Evans, 34, is an MIT grad whose latest business venture — a company similar in ambition to Theranos called Haemanthus — is also raising eyebrows. He broke his silence first with a Nov. 2 “Ask Me Anything” on X , where he addressed speculation about cocaine use (he said his drugs of choice are coffee and nicotine and that his persistent screen sniffles were the result of cedar allergies). He also denied being gay (“In 2026, being gay is considerably more socially acceptable than being in love with Elizabeth Holmes,” he wrote). He then gave a sitdown with CBS Sunday Morning over the weekend, saying he in fact loved You Can See Everything , had not consented to his nudity being shown and did not currently have plans to sue studio A24 over his depiction in the film. But Evans has a lot more to say. In his first print interview about the film, he wants to respond to Amanda Seyfried , 40, who recently told Rolling Stone that making the film, “I became this weird Billy Evans detective because I had gotten such strong negative feelings from him in the footage.” After filming their contentious dinner together, her opinion of him “only got worse.” He also disputes one of the documentary’s most consequential scenes, in which Fielder and Oppenheim depict Evans holding up production over a cut of the profits. Evans says the financial terms were agreed upon two days before filming began and appearance releases were signed shortly after. Below, Evans addresses all of that and much more, including that much-debated bag of turkey jerky, Holmes’ own thoughts on the shower scene and what, exactly, he and Holmes mean by “monuments of love.” You ready, Billy? No. Fair enough. That’s an honest answer, but I did not prep for this at all. Do you ever worry that the movie will be something your kids will have to carry for the rest of their lives? No, I don’t. Why not? At the time in which we were thinking about doing this movie, which was in February of 2023, already things were happening [to my kids], like they’d be uninvited from a play date or when we were looking at the first preschools or something. And I felt like the world had created a narrative about who their mom was that was untrue. The goal with this film is really to let people just see her and make up their own mind, which was kind of in part why we chose Nathan. He’s a genius filmmaker. He’s insanely creative and he tells a story that only he could tell. And your gut reaction after the first time seeing it — did you feel it helped or hindered your cause? I’m so biased. So I think I’m really kind of the last person whose opinion matters on the subject. But to me, when Liz is on screen — and I think it’s an important distinction to make compared to recreations or reenactments — that’s just who she is. That is Elizabeth Holmes. It’s the same Liz I saw the first day I met her and it’s the same Liz now that she’s in prison. She’s insanely trusting and kind, compassionate, a bit naive, but that’s who she is. Now the problem is that people see that and they have a hard time believing it’s real. That’s been my experience for the last decade. That’s who she really is. And what about the depiction of you? I really didn’t like it. It’s hard to see yourself depicted in a way that frames things so intensely negative, having people scrutinize the smallest of actions, like helping your wife make eggs and it being turned into some condemnation of toxic masculinity or some controlling nature. Control is a word that I’ve never really considered in my relationship with Liz. We just infinitely trust one another. Is she generally inept in the kitchen? You have to remember she was running a company for 16 years. She didn’t cook at all, at all. There’s a reason why she just had green drinks. She was unable to cook. Liz could burn water. And I grew up working in kitchens. My first job was in a kitchen, so I love cooking. When Liz was pregnant, I cooked every single meal for the two years she was pregnant for us. I’d make meals for 10, 15, 20 people every night of the trial. I love cooking. She doesn’t like it at all. Billy Evans and son Wills, LA 2024 Niki Boon There’s an expression from reality TV: “Blame it on the edit.” Do you feel that you were the victim of the edit? I actually interpret the scene very differently than everyone else because I just don’t even think about control. So that’s not how I saw it at all. I think the criticism of it and the creepy music and then the focus on it later and Amanda’s reaction to it was different than how I interpreted it. The one thing that everyone brings up first about you is the shower scene. I saw the New York Times did a whole story on it. Oh, really? Yeah. I don’t read all this stuff. Look, so much of this stuff can really just be chalked up to my naivete. I always heard about you have to sign some nudity waiver. I just assumed you can’t show people naked on screen without them consenting to it. So yes, I absolutely consented to them filming me showering, but my understanding is that they wouldn’t show [my penis] in the film. It was not like I wanted to show the world myself naked. I’ve seen people saying it was an example of you peacocking. I’m with a bunch of dudes. There was no woman on the entire production. You grow pretty close with a group of guys. Why do you think they chose to include it? You should ask them. It wasn’t my decision. I wasn’t part of the process. We had lawyers reach out to them after I had heard that it had happened, pleading for them to remove it. If it was the case that I was peacocking, I wouldn’t have asked them to take it out. And what’s Elizabeth’s opinion of that scene? She hasn’t seen the movie, but she felt strongly about it. She’s a pretty traditional person and felt that it’s a violation of our intimacy. But for me, there’s a lot of embarrassment associated with everyone you know and their moms and the kids’ parents at drop-off having seen this. Did I consent to them filming me? Yes. Did I consent to them showing it to the world? No. I would expect them to blur things. But as the film goes on, there are other scenes that are harder to explain away. Are there any that really horrified you? They were really circumstances of the situation that I’m going through. I’m not a single parent, but I am the only person that is physically with my kids five days a week and I’m raising them more or less alone. And Liz is the most incredible partner given the circumstances. She wrote two letters a day to the kids every day for the first two years she was in prison, two letters to me every day. She’s written over 3,000 letters over the course of the time she’s in prison. They are really intricate. She’ll cut up nature magazine articles that are relevant for the kids and then do these beautiful illustrations and teach them lessons through them and we read them every night. But I’m the person who’s carrying the load here and driving them out every weekend and building a business. And I moved them away from my family in San Diego to Texas so we could all be together. So I think [people need] to understand the frustrations or the anger, which certainly exists at a system in which I feel like my wife is 100 percent innocent and wrongfully incarcerated. I certainly have frustrations. Where I did start to get a little, I don’t know, concerned about you is a sequence where you talk about, first of all, always carrying a gun with you. Then you say that you “have vengeance in your heart.” I think that’s not true. What was going on when you said that? Why did you say it? Look, there’s many things that I said over the course of three and a half years that I would word so differently. There’s things that I’m embarrassed about saying or that I wish I had not said altogether. But I wasn’t thinking [at the time] about everything I said on camera. I was trying my best to open up all of me, including the bad parts in those moments of anger, sadness and frustration. The start of filming was April 24, 2023. That was a long time ago, and I’ve grown a lot as a person over that period of time. If there’s things that I’m not embarrassed about having said three and a half years ago, then I haven’t grown enough. Elizabeth Holmes and Billy Evans at home in Calif., on March 24, 2023. Philip Cheung/The New York Times/Redux Where did you see the movie, by the way? Were you with an audience? I was, yeah. They refused to show it to me before it came out. Did people in the audience recognize it was you? No. No, they didn’t. I came in right before it started. I went to the opening showtime of opening day here in Austin with a friend and her mom. I happened to be in Chicago on opening weekend, and I went to see it. It was a packed theater, and they were quite vocal. Yeah, it was strange to see people laughing at things that I didn’t think were particularly funny. It was strange to be part of an audience where there’s an audience sentiment about something that you don’t also share, or [about which] you have more context and understanding. In the film, when Amanda Seyfried, whose name I now know how to pronounce because of the film… I learned it there, too. But before she even meets you, based on the footage she sees, she’s very vocal about the fact that she doesn’t like you, she doesn’t trust you, and she thinks you’re a bad influence on your wife. Yeah, that was very strange to see. I heard women behind me in Chicago cheering her on and clapping and saying “exactly,” as if she voiced what they had been thinking all along. Amanda becomes an avatar for everyone who doesn’t like you while they’re watching the movie. She recently doubled and tripled down on that, telling Rolling Stone that when she finally met you, she thought worse of you. How do you respond to that? I’ve heard she was going through a lot in her life at the time in which this was being filmed, so I can understand why she’d view our relationship through a different lens than reality. I’d also say that she’s never spent any time with me and Liz together, and what she saw was not raw footage. She saw the edit that the audience saw. And by “going through” things, you mean her own divorce? I don’t know. I see a lot of headlines. I’d rather not comment on specifics. What I can say is Elizabeth and I have been through enormous challenges that people have read about — and some harder things that nobody knows about. Through that process, our relationship has only become stronger than it’s ever been. That’s a great testament to the love that we do have for each other, and it doesn’t matter much to me what other people think about it, because they don’t see it. They see small vignettes stitched together with music, being told by an A-list or B-list celebrity what to think about it. But it’s my life and I love it. I’m super happy. I’ve got this incredible family. We’ve got this amazing tribe of people who have been through hell and back with us, who support us through every one of those challenges. And I’ve got two beautiful children that I get to spend every day with. If other people are unhappy about our relationship, I suggest that they invest more time in their own. What’s your version of how it went down, what we saw on screen, where it gets quite contentious across the dinner table? It made more sense to me after seeing the film, and hearing her say, “I want to break them up.” I didn’t understand her intentions [when she came over]. I thought we were extending an olive branch and saying, “Look, we’re not angry with you. We’re happy to engage. We don’t blame you for your portrayal of Liz [in The Dropout ]. You’re an actress, you didn’t write the script, you didn’t develop the story, you didn’t do the research or lack thereof.” What about this notion that she has something to gain personally from portraying Elizabeth? She won an Emmy for The Dropout , and they’re now saying she’s up for an Oscar for You Can See Everything . Yeah. It seems there is an unwillingness to confront the reality of the consequences of playing a living person, especially when you readily admit 80 percent of it was made up. Then you say, “Well, but I’m really good at playing her and people can’t distinguish the difference between me and her.” Which is it? When confronted, you say it’s just a story, it’s entertainment, it’s just made up. Then when trying to convince Nathan to [cast you in a role], you say, “People can’t tell the difference between me and her.” I think that’s kind of an interesting and very fluid interpretation. But back to the dinner. You’re saying when you saw the film, you realized she came in with the intention to break you two up. What prompted your remarks about Charlie Kirk and her career? I’m not going to be able to recreate the exact exchange from years ago for you. I can tell you that this was not just a random burst of frustration. She clearly states her intention in the film and she lived up to that intention, but it obviously didn’t work. She had a theory that you were controlling Elizabeth through — what’s the legal term that you had over her? Power of attorney. Yeah, I think it’s important to talk about that for a minute. It shows her complete lack of understanding of the legal system. She’s like, “But she’s still alive!” Yeah, power of attorney is not relevant if somebody is dead. That is called a will. Power of attorney is unfortunately a requirement of being incarcerated, in our case. We’ve got two kids, we’re not married. If I need to make big decisions, that’s a way in which I can do so. I’ve got no ability to contact Elizabeth immediately when a decision or something needs to be made. There’s decisions, like picking a legal team, in which she cannot meet with them until we set up the first conversations. And I need to be able to talk to them to understand, is this somebody that we want to work with or not? And there’s other examples — like her cell phone number. If I didn’t have access to her bank account or her cell phone bill, I wouldn’t be able to make the payment on her behalf. That decision was made between Elizabeth and I over the course of months. Like the idea of being on X. The film criticizes me for speaking on her behalf, but I would point to the fact that Nathan is speaking on her behalf through the reenactments that he makes. Amanda is speaking on her behalf by voicing those words and has done so in the past. I am a third person doing it, but I’m the only person with her explicit authority and consent and knowledge. They don’t have that. Well, once we’re on this topic, what about the whole tweet thing? Well, that’s in part what I’m talking about. Liz and I talked about this. If you look at Liz’s profile on X, it’s remained unchanged since the first day we relaunched her X account in August of ’25. It says “founder of Theranos,” and then at the bottom it says, “mostly my words posted by others.” We’ve been very clear about the fact that everything posted on our X account is not just her words from the very beginning. And that was a decision. We worded that purposely together. That in itself wouldn’t bother me. But then they start showing these hostile tweets with swear words in them. And then it’s like, well, that’s a little weird. Did it strike you as weird? Yeah, but it’s Twitter. This isn’t a State of the Union address. And you look at the examples that are given, it’s like in response to somebody asking for the 10th time if you can show them your feet and if you’re starting an OnlyFans account or if you’re going to start a crypto token. Right. But you could just ignore that. Especially because she is a former CEO and is currently incarcerated. I am not an expert at this stuff. Do I wish I would have hired some masterful team to help do this properly? Absolutely. But I was doing the best I can. I certainly made mistakes throughout the process. There’s some element of shitposting and joking about these things. You have to remember the environment on X is where politicians and the White House press secretary or White House chief of communication or lots of powerful people who have really important positions are using similar language because of the audience and because of where it’s being said. They would not say that in a press conference. They would not say that in a shareholder letter. I think the context is important to remember. I think it’s kind of ironic that there’s so much of a focus on me saying “F— you” to somebody. And then in the film, they’re recreating something that absolutely did not happen categorically, recreating a scene suggesting that Elizabeth and I are jumping up and down saying “we got the fucking money.” [The interview pauses for Evans to take a call from Holmes.] Billy Evans and children Wills and Ivy, LA 2024 Niki Boon What’s the frequency of her calling? She has 510 minutes a month on the phone, which is split between me and everyone else. If you go one second over, then it takes a whole minute from you. Before she called, you had brought up the recreation of the pizza party negotiation with A24. So tell me, what were we misled with there? What didn’t happen? The entire thing. Nathan says something in the film to the effect of “we had to move quickly, so we started filming before they had signed an appearance release and they refused to sign anything before we had this meeting in Los Angeles at one of his friends’ houses.” Was there any meeting with any A24 executive? Yes, there were. There were two senior people from A24. Was one of them [A24 CEO] Daniel Katz? No, not that senior. We’re not that big of a deal. It was at my friend’s house, but it was a one-story house. So this whole idea that Liz goes upstairs or something, I know it seems like a small detail, but I was at the house the other night. There’s no pretending like you’re in a completely separate room or hiding behind doors. That’s completely fictitious. The way it’s depicted in the film is that it’s not clear when she stepped away from the table if she knew or didn’t know that you were about to ask for a percentage of the film’s profits. On April 16, 2023, Nathan and Lance came down to San Diego. The way in which we had connected with them was through one of the producers on the project who went to high school with some of my friends. I knew him from college. His name is Jack Davis. It’s not a mystery. It was my idea to make a movie. This was not something that she was planning to do or was really thinking about. I had spoken to a lot of different people about this — maybe 10 different documentary filmmakers and people that I thought could help tell the story. A24 was one of those groups. That introduction had come through Jack. So Nathan and Lance then come down to San Diego on April 16, which is depicted in the film as a recreation in which Nathan is talking about David Blaine. That actually happened. On April 18, A24 made its first financial offer. On April 19, we met again in Los Angeles at my friend’s house. I wanted Nathan and Lance to know that that was on the table. On April 21, that’s the first documented transmission of an appearance release. On April 22, commercial terms, including the backend, were agreed to. Then it was handed over to the lawyers. We signed the releases a few weeks later. So there was never a conversation where Fielder objected and said, “You can’t make a proper documentary if you’re getting paid?” I do recall them saying, “This is atypical,” but it was not a big deal. I mean, the entire conversation maybe lasted two minutes, and they immediately said, “OK.” And then from there, it was just handed off to the team. And then we started filming on April 24. But this idea that we were “holding up” signing an appearance release and they had already started filming is completely made up. If they didn’t think it was ethical or if they didn’t think it was fair or if they thought it was improper, they could have walked away from it. A big thing is made in the film of her saying, “I’m not getting paid for this.” She was not. I was. So what Liz said was true. What she said is, “I am not profiting in any way from this.” We are completely financially distinct. We are not married. We keep our assets separate. It was the most stressful period of our life by far. [When they brought it up again three years later,] it was really hard for me to remember what Liz knew, what I knew, what the lawyers handled, what they told me after the fact. I couldn’t remember clearly, and I still don’t. I answered to the best of my ability. They could have very easily just not made the movie. Instead they attempt to villainize me in that negotiation and recreation, and I think it takes up way too much of the movie, and I think it’s just so uninteresting. There’s a title card at the end, a chyron, that says you relinquished your piece of the backend. Is that true? That is a true statement. When did you relinquish it? They said “shortly after filming.” I can check the exact dates, but it was maybe five months ago. It suggests that I knew filming was completed. I didn’t. I thought that they were going to continue filming [past Elizabeth’s release]. Why did you do that? They said that it would help the project. Time and time again, when there’s things that I really didn’t want to do that they said would be helpful for making a better movie and helping people see Liz more clearly, I made those sacrifices or decisions to help the project. I have to be honest, I’m surprised you capitulated to that. You seem like a stubborn guy. I am totally stubborn, but if there’s anything that I can do to help Liz regardless of the cost, I will do it. Did you consult with her before you made that decision? She was OK with neither of us getting paid from the very beginning. I mean, she didn’t have a strong opinion one way or another. Her problems are so much bigger than this and she really doesn’t care about money. I’m a little bit more of a realist. At the time in which these things were negotiated, I’m a single dad with two kids whose best friend’s about to be sent to prison. And at that time I didn’t have a job. I’m trying to provide for my family and I’m really scared about what’s to come. Could we talk about the prison sequence at the end of the film? Let me ask about something kind of silly, but that I’ve seen debated, which is in the last shot of the film you’re seen sharing or eating from the bag of turkey jerky that Nathan supposedly bought for her. I’ve seen it interpreted in different ways. One is that you’re eating her turkey jerky and how selfish could you be? That just shows how people want to see me. The machines have a lot of every item in them. I’ve got a credit card and I’ve probably spent tens of thousands of dollars on nuts and snacks over the course of the last three and a half years that we were there. I can tell you what I think happened, which is ironic because the turkey jerky’s name is Think. I actually got reached out to by the CEO of the turkey jerky company telling me, “Thank you. Our sales have increased so much and this is awesome. I really appreciate it.” And then they tried to drop off a big box of turkey jerky at a place that used to be our office. She loves E0 on the vending machine all the way to the left, and she loves the nuts, which are E9 all the way to the right, because they have banana chips in them. I can remember a handful of times over that period that Liz requested turkey jerky, just a handful. What’s E0? E0 is a different type of trail mix that has some pieces of dehydrated fruit in it. So I know the system well. Another important detail is none of the vending machines have clocks on them. I checked again last weekend. None of them have clocks on them. Nathan says he saw the time on the vending machine. That’s impossible. My guess is I got turkey jerky for myself. Nathan added that detail into their reenactment scene together to create continuity in the film. And there’s this other theory that Nathan is depicting a romantic rivalry, because then it cuts to them frolicking in the surf. Could he be that devious? I think devious is the wrong word, but I think Nathan’s an excellent storyteller and a lot of this film is different than the truth. A lot of it’s to create an entertaining product that drives ticket sales, and they’ve been incredibly successful at that. They sort of crafted the perfect Reddit entertainment. Yeah, they did a phenomenal job of it. But the truth is they could have made a very similar movie about many different people. From left: Elizabeth Holmes, Billy Evans and Nathan Fielder in ‘You Can See Everything.’ Lance Oppenheim One thing I came away with is that you hoped that the movie would recast Liz from a villain in prison to what you see as the loving, compassionate woman that is mother to your children. And in that sense, it kind of worked. Because look what we’re talking about. You’re the bad guy now. I’m willing to take any arrows for people to see her. I just wish that more time had been spent with her and on her rather than on my negotiation with the filmmakers or picking apart a word from three years ago or making eggs. Nathan and Lance made a beautiful film and they told a really compelling story. It just really differs from the reality that I experienced. I think in the parts in which Liz is on camera, they do a beautiful job of depicting her. You speak in the film of building monuments of love to each other. That’s a new phrase. I’ve never heard that in my life. What were you referring to? Nathan asked something to the effect of, “Well, what would she say if she was here right now?” And what I say is, “If she was here, she’d tell you that in 500 years she’d be remembered for this love story and that she’ll dedicate her life to building monuments of love to me.” When I say it, it sounds like the most narcissistic and self-serving thing on the planet, and it looks crazy. And then he goes and sees her and she repeats it nearly verbatim. That’s just how she describes us. I’m just asking what it means. That we are deeply in love and deeply connected and really plugged into one another. But what’s a monument to love? That’s my question. What does that mean to you? We have all these ideas of things that we want to do with our life to come. We’re deeply committed to improving human health and reducing suffering. Liz and I watched this Anthony Bourdain episode on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Anthony’s going down the river and slaughtering a chicken trying to clean it. He’s just getting eaten alive by mosquitoes, and he eventually shows up to this kind of abandoned banana research and fruit research farm that was built by the French in the ’60s or something, and it’s completely falling apart. Liz and I have talked about building an infectious disease research station there and dedicating it to one another. That’s a monument to love. I’ve seen a lot of discussion regarding Elizabeth’s father, Christian Holmes IV, and a revelation about her which you interrupted. Her parents are some of my best friends. I’ve spent an enormous amount of time with them over the course of the last nine years. In the film, they make it look like her parents are disgusted with me or with Liz and what we’re talking about before she goes. They’re just scared. Their daughter’s going to prison. They have no idea how to handle this. There’s a part in the film in which they’re talking to Liz’s dad and he says, “I’ll tell you where something went wrong or where everything changed: It’s when she was raped at Stanford.” Then the film just drops it and never engages with it again. I’ve even had friends ask me, “Well, why did you cut them off?” Liz had two days before she went to prison, and we were trying to find a balance between access and preserving time with family, and there was no perfect balance there. Lance and Nathan spent significant time with her parents interviewing them and going through high school video and teacher reports from middle school trying to understand who Liz was. If they wanted to know what Chris meant in saying that, they had an infinite opportunity to explore it, but they didn’t put it in the film because they chose not to. It’s funny though, because you never fully condemn Nathan and Lance. You often say they made a beautiful film, they did this, they did that, they’re brilliant. But then at the same time you say it was deceptive and they had bad intentions. I don’t know if I said they had bad intentions. Well, bad in that they were creating a narrative at your expense. I think it shows the frailty of memory. [In the reenactments] I think he’s just trying to convey it to the best of his recollection. But I think those memories aren’t that great, man. Has Liz relayed to you how the success of this film is affecting her life in prison? Yeah, but I’d have to go off the record and tell you about that. I think what I can say on record is that it’s been really hard since the film has come out. Does it feel weird to be in the movie of the year that’s in Oscar contention, maybe even front-runner status, and being the most compelling character in that film? It is so weird. It’s hard to describe to you, and I think I’m still trying to work through how I feel about it. If you ask me the same questions in six months, I might have different answers for you about how I feel about things. I’m willing to take on new information, make a new opinion. I’m trying to explain to you how I feel in this moment, and it’s a really strange moment. And it’s kind of exacerbated by the fact that I can’t talk to my best friend about it because she hasn’t seen it. That’s the weirdest part in this to me. I’ve described things to her, but she hasn’t seen any of it. Billy Evans with Wills and Ivy, LA 2024 Niki Boon THR

title: Gotham Film Awards To Honor ‘Being Heumann’ With Ensemble Tribute
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Patrick Hipes Patrick Hipes Executive Managing Editor More Stories By Patrick Gotham Film Awards To Honor ‘Being Heumann’ With Ensemble Tribute Danny Boyle Talks ‘Ink’, The Common Architecture Of His Movies And More ‘28 Years Later’ As He Receives The Deadline Legend Award Danny Boyle Says Tabloid Headlines Censored In British Version Of ‘Ink’ Will Be Shown In U.S. View All November 17, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Being Heumann' Michael Gibson / Apple TV / Everett Collection EXCLUSIVE: Apple Original Films’ Being Heumann has been selected to receive the Gotham Ensemble Tribute at the 36th annual Gotham Film Awards later this month. Ruth Madeley stars as Judy Heumann in Oscar-winning co-writer/director Siân Heder’s true-life story about Heumann, who in 1977 with a rag-tag coalition of disability-rights advocates take over the San Francisco Federal Building in what would become the longest occupation in U.S. history. Mark Ruffalo plays the bureaucrat in their way of their goal of broader civil rights protections for people with disabilities. Related Stories News Gotham Awards Film Nominations Led By ‘The Invite’, ‘Tender Loving Care’, ‘All Of A Sudden’ & More News ‘Being Heumann’ Star Ruth Madeley And Casting Team On Championing Diversity Onscreen – Contenders L.A. The cast that will be honored by the Gothams also includes Madeline Delp, Roberta Colindrez, Jon Beavers, Antwan Tolliver, Ray Fisher, Andrew Pilkington, Michael Patrick Thornton, Russell Harvard, Daniel Durant, Charlie Rush-Reese, Rio Finnegan, D’Arcee Charington Neal, Will Brill, Rob Delaney, Matthew August Jeffers, Siena Rafter, Rein Barcel, Stephen Adly Guirgis and Dylan O’Brien. Watch on Deadline The Ensemble Tribute recognizes casts “whose artistry and chemistry captivate audiences on the big screen.” Last year’s recipient was eventual Oscar Best Picture nominee Sinners . “Ruth Madeley and the cast of Being Heumann bring a pivotal chapter in the disability rights movement to life, capturing the determination of activists who demanded and secured lasting change,” said Jeffrey Sharp, Executive Director of The Gotham Film & Media Institute. “The Gothams have been proud to champion Siân Heder’s storytelling since honoring CODA in 2021. We’re thrilled to recognize Ruth’s commanding performance and this exceptional cast with The Gotham Ensemble Tribute.” Being Heumann opened this year’s Toronto Film Festival before hitting theaters November 6. It began streaming on Apple TV on November 13. Heder, an Oscar winner for CODA , adapted the screenplay with Rebekah Taussig based on Heumann’s memoir. The pic joins Ellen Burstyn (Performer Tribute), Elsinore (Legacy Tribute), Michael (Musical Tribute), La Bola Negra (Vanguard Tribute), Ink helmer Danny Boyle (Director Tribute) and Wildwood studio Laika (Anniversary Tribute) on the honorees list for the Gotham Film Awards ceremony, set for November 30 at Cipriani Wall Street in New York City. title: Kira Goldberg Leaving Netflix As VP Film To Join Paramount As President Of Motion Picture Group Alongside Don Granger; WB’s Jesse Ehrman Upped
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Kira Goldberg Leaving Netflix As VP Film To Join Paramount As President Of Motion Picture Group Alongside Don Granger; WB’s Jesse Ehrman Upped Nicolas Cage & Chris Pine To Star In Vegas Drama Series ‘American Epic’ From B.J. Novak & A24 ‘Reasonable Doubt’ Gets Early Season 5 Renewal As Season 4 Becomes Hulu Series’ Most Watched View All November 17, 2026 8:50am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Story Arc L-R: Kira Goldberg, Don Granger, Jesse Ehrman Courtesy Kira Goldberg is departing Netflix where she has been for eight years, most recently as VP Film, Faith, Holiday, YA, and Family. She is headed to Paramount Pictures , where she will take on a top position alongside Don Granger, who will maintain his current title. Both will now be Presidents, Motion Picture Group, reporting to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, Co-Chairs, Motion Picture Group at Skydance . Goldberg’s appointment is part of a broader restructuring of the Skydance Motion Picture Group unveiled Tuesday morning by Dana Goldberg and Greenstein in an internal memo, which you can read below. Related Stories News Jeff Goldstein Exits As Global Theatrical Distribution Boss After 48-Year Warner Bros Run Executives Jennifer Dodge and Traci Balthazor To Oversee Animation Across Both Paramount And Warner Bros As Bill Damaschke Departs On the Warner Bros side, 20-year studio veteran Jesse Ehrman has been elevated to President, Motion Picture Group. As President of Production and Development, he was the most senior executive at the studio following the exit last month of Warner Bros. Motion Picture Co-Chairs and CEOs Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy . Watch on Deadline With Kira Goldberg, Granger and Ehrman, Dana Goldberg and Greenstein have established a top layer of creative executives at Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros Pictures as the duo take on the bigger responsibility of overseeing the merged company’s entire motion picture operation. Michael Ireland will continue as President of Production, reporting to Ehrman. Word about Kira Goldberg’s departure from Netflix started spreading Tuesday morning when she notified the staff, sources said. The exit comes a month after the shakeup at Netflix, where Peter Rice joined as new Chief Content Officer , followed by the exit of Dan Lin as Head of Film just a few days later. His position remains vacant. Goldberg’s departure also comes four months after she was promoted , adding live-action family film to her portfolio. In her most recent role, Goldberg oversaw Netflix films in the genres of Drama, Thriller, Holiday, and Family, including hit Apex and crowd pleasers Remarkably Bright Creatures and The Life List . Coming up from Goldberg’s slate are Heartland , starring Jessica Chastain; Bad Day, starring Cameron Diaz; Here Comes the Flood, starring Denzel Washington, Robert Pattinson and Daisy Edgar-Jones; Positano , starring Matthew McConaughey and Zoe Saldaña; An Innocent Girl, starring Kerry Washington and James Marsden; and inspirational sports drama The 99ers . Goldberg joined Netflix in 2018 as Director, Original Studio Film, upped to VP the following year, overseeing Don’t Look Up, The Mother and Leave the World Behind among others. Prior to Netflix, Goldberg served as EVP of Production at Fox and as VP of Production at DreamWorks. Here is Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein’s memo: Team, The theatrical business is central to the company’s vision for the future of Skydance. We are home to more than a century of extraordinary storytelling, legendary films and an enduring impact on audiences and culture around the world. We have both an incredible legacy to build upon and an enormous opportunity ahead of us: to champion the world’s best filmmakers, invest in ambitious storytelling and deliver an unparalleled slate of films that captivate audiences everywhere. As we shape this next chapter for Skydance, we want to share the leadership structure for the film divisions that comprise the Skydance Motion Picture Group. We said it on day one: Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures are our cornerstone labels and will remain distinct. Both will continue to anchor our biggest commercial and filmmaker-driven projects, with our animation and specialty labels also remaining separate with their own creative mandates. Our leadership structure is designed to empower each studio and label with dedicated creative leadership, backed by an excellent corporate team that provides the expertise, resources and support to help them succeed. Together, we are building an organization with the creative ambition, resources and scale to deliver on our commitment of 30 films per year. Studios Business Leadership Our corporate team brings collective expertise across key operations that ultimately support our creative output. The team comprises Courtney Armstrong, Chief Operating Officer; Mark Badagliacca, Chief Financial Officer; Brooke Robertson, EVP, Head of Global Communications & Media Relations; and Talia Robinson, EVP, Human Resources. Josh Goldstine has been named President of Worldwide Marketing and Distribution. Shaun Barber and Mark Viane will continue to report to Josh and oversee domestic and international distribution for both Paramount and Warner Bros. Jeff Goldstein, who has worked on over 1,000 films over 48 years of an illustrious career, will retire and transition into a consulting role. Jeff is a stalwart of this industry, and as we align these two organizations, his counsel will be tremendous. Additionally, Josh Silverman, President, Global Products & Publishing, will transition to our group to lead Consumer Products and Publishing, which will add important connectivity between our stable of IP and a key revenue stream. Mark Kaufman, EVP & Chief Content Officer, Theatre Ventures, will now report to Josh, where he will continue overseeing an acclaimed portfolio, including the Tony-winning Broadway production of The Lost Boys. Separately, we want to let you know that Ted Lim will be departing the company. We thank him for his leadership and contributions as Chief Business Officer and wish him all the best. Creative Leadership Paramount Pictures Don Granger and Kira Goldberg will lead Paramount Pictures as Presidents, Motion Picture Group. Over the last year, Don has been a great partner as we’ve repositioned the studio, bringing in key talent relationships and nearly doubling output. As our slate continues to grow, so does our team, and we’re thrilled to welcome Kira. Most recently at Netflix, she oversaw a slate that included Don’t Look Up , starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence, and the upcoming Bad Day with Cameron Diaz and The Take starring Denzel Washington and Robert Pattinson. Before that, she worked on films including Bohemian Rhapsody, The Post and The Greatest Showman during her tenure at Fox. Together, Don and Kira will work hand in hand going forward. Warner Bros. Pictures Jesse Ehrman has been elevated to President, Motion Picture Group. With over 20 years at Warner Bros., Jesse has been instrumental in many of the studio’s biggest hits including recent movies like A Minecraft Movie and Sinners , and has built lasting relationships with the studio’s most important filmmakers. Michael Ireland will continue as President of Production, reporting to Jesse. Mike’s relationships across the industry, strong eye for material and leadership experience make him an integral part of the motion picture group. DC Studios As we recently announced, Jeremy Latcham is joining us as President and Chief Creative Officer of DC Studios. James Gunn and Peter Safran will step away from their leadership roles after four years transforming and resetting the studio’s foundation and return full time to their creative work. Animation As part of this restructuring, Bill Damaschke will exit Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, and has agreed to stay for a period of time until he transitions to full-time producing. We thank him for his dedication to the animation business and greatly respect his commitment to this craft. In the interim, Jennifer Dodge and Traci Balthazor will oversee all animation across both Paramount and Warner Bros. Pictures, while Chris Leahy will continue to oversee the day-to-day operations of Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, reporting into Jennifer and Traci. John Lasseter remains Head of Skydance Animation alongside Holly Edwards, President, Skydance Animation. Specialty Labels and Divisions Our specialty labels and divisions will be led by Richard Brener, President, Chief Content Officer, New Line; Lia Buman, EVP, Head of Global Acquisitions and Republic Pictures; J.D. Lifshitz and Raphael Margules, Heads of Paramount Primal; Christian Parkes, Head of Clockwork; and Charlie Tabesh, SVP and General Manager, Turner Classic Movies. This team brings deep knowledge of our businesses, strong creative instincts and longstanding relationships across the industry. We have tremendous confidence in these leaders and are grateful for their partnership. Our shared responsibility is to give our filmmakers, storytellers and teams the support they need to do their best work. As we continue to build out the broader organization, this leadership structure establishes a strong foundation for the work ahead. We know how much work is underway across the company, and we’re grateful for the care, focus and dedication you bring to it every day. We look forward to all that we will build and accomplish together. title: ‘Survivor 51’ Star Kristin Flickinger on Her Chaotic Exit, Being an Unexpected Threat and Overwhelming Fan Response
full_text: Continue to The Hollywood Reporter SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Terry Terrones Plus Icon Terry Terrones @terryterrones Follow Sign Up View All November 17, 2026 8:49am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kristin Flickinger Robert Voets/CBS ©2026 CBS Broadcasting, Inc. All Rights Reserved. Logo text Kristin Flickinger waited 26 years to play Survivor , and when she finally got her chance, she proved that all those years of preparation weren’t for nothing. From her impressive survival skills to navigating the game with a broken foot, Kristin quickly established herself as one of Survivor 51’s most memorable castaways. But despite spending decades studying the game, there was one thing she never anticipated: being considered a social threat. That reputation, combined with a chaotic Tribal Council featuring multiple twists and advantages, ultimately brought her long-awaited adventure to an end. Related Stories TV 'Cupertino' Moving, 'Ghosts' Doubling Up on CBS' Midseason Schedule TV Kids' Choice Awards: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day,' Zendaya, Tom Holland, BTS Among 2026 Winners In an exclusive interview with The Hollywood Reporter , Kristin opens up about her elimination, why pairing with Kilby was a strategic misstep and the overwhelmingly positive response she’s received from fans. She also reflects on her decades-long pursuit of a spot on the show and shares a hilarious behind-the-scenes story involving a boat, a broken foot and a whole lot of waving. *** At one point at Tribal Council you ask, “Is anyone playing the game they thought they were gonna play?” which I found interesting. Where or when did your game take a detour from your plans? I studied for a long time and I studied with the thinking that I’ll just get all of this knowledge, and then I can kind of toss away any plans and be fluid and pull on all of the different parts of my understanding of the game. And I did that. I went out with a half a vote with four intersecting, interlocking wild twists. So I feel good about that. But I think what I was referring to then was that I thought I would come in and be this huge thinky presence, which in some ways I was. I didn’t think I would be a social threat. Even now, I can’t even say it. A social threat is not what I thought was going to happen. So when people were like, “You’re just too liked,” I don’t know what to do with that, man. All I’m doing is showing up and being myself and doing too much. And people saw me as a social threat. So it was confusing to me and I didn’t know how to get out of that because I had never planned for that. It’s permanent uncertainty. I think a lot of folks went in thinking they were going to play a certain way and it’s very hard to do when you don’t know what’s coming. For me, I begged for this. I wanted to be on 51 because I thought a lot of people are going to think something new is happening, but they won’t know what the new is. Then I can tell them what the new is and I can convince them of it and I’ll have a strategic advantage. And then it was even better than that because it was the theme of the season. But everybody out there was thinking like me. Everybody came to play. Everyone understood the assignment. This cast is fire. It is just nonstop from start to finish, nonstop. You went home because of a single vote: Devin’s. Does that make the loss easier to accept because you had a good read on where everyone stood, or harder because your fate came down to one person’s decision? Half a vote. I think for some folks it might be harder. For me, this was an iconic vote out. It was an epic Tribal Council. It was Adventageddon 2.0. Does it make it easy to go out? I’m not sure anyone would be like, “Yeah, that was easy.” No, I think it’s hard to go out and after 26 years, really hard to go out. At the same time, I had been segregated from everyone. I was the only person that went to Tribal Council once pre-merge. People were building by attrition. I had to build by addition. So people were going and voting folks out and they were coming back together and understanding where they were. I didn’t have that. I had to be working with everyone. I had to try to work with Maggie. I had a long conversation with Dev. I had a long conversation with Lewis. I had long conversations that day with people I’d never talked to. So to see for me that that paid off and I had this one vote that was smart to play. They split the vote. That’s a smart thing to do. They thought I had something. Okay, I didn’t have something, but I knew that I needed to play my shot in the dark. I understood that intuitively. You play your best. Luck happens in Survivor . I’ve studied this game a long time. I know luck is a part of it, so luck comes into play, that’s fair. Let’s go back to when you guys learned about the duo twist. How did you know what it was and walk me through the process of how you ended up with Kilby and why not immediately pair up with Sharonda because of the tethered idol? We knew what it was because we were made aware of a couple of the twists in the season. We were made aware of what Double Duos was. We were made aware of Coin Flip. So we knew that those things had played in 50. You’ll hear me in my confessional say, “It’s either we’re playing together or we’re going to compete against each other.” That was because also I watched Drag Race and I know from year to year, they’ll swap it around. So I was like, I don’t know which one this is, girl. Let’s get ready. In terms of getting paired up with Kilby, at that point I knew that my threat level was skyrocketing. People thought I had not one idol, but multiple idols. I tried to turn that down my threat level when I came back from Exile and I told them that I had gotten a build your own fake immunity idol kit. I told them that I made an idol out of beads I’d stolen from the Savu flag when I was laid up with a broken foot in camp. I brought it back, I told them, I put it down in camp and they said, “Don’t touch it. It’s probably a cursed idol.” So my threat level, no matter what I did, was just increasing. But why not pair up with Sharonda instead of Kilby? At that point I put my hand up and I said, “Hey guys, I know that I’m not great physically right now with my broken foot. If anyone wants to pair up with me, that would be so nice. I’m still good at puzzles.” And Kilby raised his hand and said, “I’ll pair up with you, Kristin.” And it was like, “Oh no,” because Kilby was not at the top of anyone’s list, but he was absolutely a threat. He was a strategic threat. He was a social threat, and he had pissed some people off. The two of us together I knew was a problem. We were just too plum a target. You couldn’t have pretended you didn’t hear him and then just started walking away? I was in the hammock with Jelly when this all went down and I was like, “Okay, Kilbs, let’s see whoever anybody else wants to pair up with.” And then I turned to Jelly and Devin was like, “I’ll take Jelly.” And I was trying to get Sharonda’s eye, strategically. I very rarely did anything that wasn’t very strategic. This one just didn’t pay off. Of all the players this season, you were the most prepared. You knew how to make a fire, what to eat, and seemed at ease on the island. Is that why players saw you as a “white whale” or was it something else they were picking up on? I mean, you’d have to ask them. I studied my butt off, and this is also just me. I went out there, I tried to not do so much. There were times when I kind of pulled back a little bit, but I wanted to provide for people because I wanted to keep us strong, especially in the tribe portion of the game. I wanted us to be strong so we could compete. But it’s hard to say, I don’t know. My partner was like, “You are going to walk in and they’re going see you as a threat.” And honestly, that’s my life. This is nothing new. People see me as a threat when I walk in the room. That’s okay. Over time, I figured out how to deal with that. There are times when people are just like, “That person’s too much of a threat.” I walked away thinking I will never again try to manage people’s concern about whether I’m a threat. My threat level, I really don’t care what people think about it in life. I could have played always as a threat and said, “I’ve got four idols come at me.” And it wouldn’t have changed anything in terms of how people perceived me. I’m pretty certain you’re the first player to get a montage of applying for Survivor for 20+ years. You didn’t get the title of Sole Survivor but you impacted the game. Was your experience what you were hoping for? I felt like my playing was a love letter to something that I love deeply. It was a love letter to the game, and it felt like a love letter back with that montage. I have those videos. I have the VHS tapes. I’ve saved them forever because they’re precious to me. This journey is precious to me, and it was precious before I got out there. I had a 25-year survivor journey before I ever played. I learned so much through the application processes. I learned so much thinking about my life in terms of survivor. Maybe that’s really toxic to Survivoriize your whole life. I don’t freaking know. But yeah, it was worth it. It was incredible. I would wait another 26 years. I really, hope I don’t have to, but it was a beautiful, beautiful experience. I don’t take any of it for granted. I’m so unbelievably grateful. And when I came out of the game, honestly, I was euphoric. I was joyful and grateful in a way that I have rarely experienced. What does it feel like to want to be on the show and applying for so long and for your personality to resonate with so many people? It’s wild. I had a great journey before, and then I got to play the game, which was everything. It was everything. I got to go to Exile Island. I communed with the islands. It was everything. And then I came out and I got to watch it on television, and I know that it’s television and you can’t show everything, and I thought those two experiences might not match up completely. They matched up a lot, and I also don’t take that for granted. I’m so grateful for that. And then to see myself, the way that I experience myself and the way that I experienced myself in the game is a gift that not everyone gets. Then to have people respond to that positively, I planned for what to do with negative feedback. I planned for how to stay off of social media and not get taken down with it. I did not plan for what it would be like to receive 99.9% positive feedback. So it’s overwhelming. It’s really overwhelming, honestly. I’m so, so grateful. Would you like a behind the scenes exclusive? Of course! Okay, for the Summit. This is a funny, this is a silly one, but when I got selected for the Summit, I was so excited. I walked down to the boat to get on and go out, and the boat was out a little ways, so I waded out up to my knees, and I was waving to everybody. I was waiting, I was waving, and I was waiting for the boat to come in. I don’t know how long I stood there. I probably said goodbye to everybody and waved five times before I realized I had to walk out to the boat. I looked ridiculous. And then I had to wade far out there, and I had a broken foot, and it’s up to my waist. So I went to the back of the boat where it was not moving as much and hoisted myself up. I was like, oh my God. title: Raúl Esparza Missing Two Days Of Broadway’s ‘Galileo’ After Suffering Concussion During Rehearsal; Michael Park Stepping In
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg John Malkovich & Rosalind Eleazar Set For West End Production Of New Play ‘History’ Jon Stewart Coulda Been A Bond Contender But The FAA, Riverboats & Robert Pattinson Got In The Way ‘The Fantasticks’ Review: A Welcome Broadway Debut Seven Decades In The Making View All November 17, 2026 8:48am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Raúl Esparza in 'Galileo'; Michael Park Kevin Berne/Production Raúl Esparza is on a two-day leave of absence from his starring role in the Broadway musical Galileo after suffering what he says was a “minor concussion” during a recent rehearsal. Michael Park ( Stranger Things, As the World Turns ), the production’s alternate Galileo, filled in for Esparza last night and will do so again tonight. Esparza is expected back tomorrow. In an Instagram video posted yesterday evening, Esparza says, “Unfortunately, I’m not going to be able to join you for performances of Galileo tonight and tomorrow. The Saturday before we started performances, I suffered a minor concussion in rehearsals, and I still wanted to go on and still wanted to do the show, and it was an amazing week, and I wouldn’t have missed it for the world. Related Stories News 'The Fantasticks' Review: A Welcome Broadway Debut Seven Decades In The Making News Bryan Cranston & Marianne Jean-Baptiste Heading To Broadway In Ivo Van Hove's Acclaimed 'All My Sons' Revival Watch the video below. Watch on Deadline “But now,” he continues, “out of an abundance of caution and per doctor’s orders, because I’m stubborn and I have to listen to them, I’m going to have to take a little bit of time off to to get better. Everything’s going to be cool. I cannot wait to join you all and join the cast of this amazing musical. It’s just been one of the most extraordinary weeks of my entire life, getting to share this with audiences, and I can’t wait to have so many more. And I’ll see you all real soon.” Galileo began performances at the Shubert Theatre on November 10 (the rehearsal during which Esparza suffered the concussion was November 7). During the show’s first week of previews, the musical was a near sell-out, grossing $710,252 for five performances. Park’s previous Broadway credits include, among others, C arousel, Smokey Joe’s Cafe, Little Me, How To Succeed In Business Without Really Trying, Cat On A Hot Tin Roof, Tuck Everlasting, Dear Evan Hansen and, most recently, 2025’s Redwood . The show’s synopsis: The synopsis: “When luminary Galileo (Esparza) peers into the heavens, what he sees challenges humanity’s understanding of the world. Unwilling to deny the truth, Galileo finds himself in a fight with the most powerful institution on Earth. As his trusted confidant Barberini (Kushnier) ascends to power, friendship leads to betrayal, and the dreams Galileo has envisioned for himself and for his brilliant daughter Virginia (Woods) begin to slip away. Belief, ambition, and love pull the trio out of orbit, each confronting what they’re willing to sacrifice for what matters most.” In addition to Esparza and Park, the musical features Jeremy Kushnier, Joy Woods, Bradley Dean, Jordon Lee Garcia and Javier Muñoz. Opening night is Sunday, December 6. Galileo features a book by Danny Strong and an original score by Zoe Sarnak and Michael Weiner, and is directed by Michael Mayer and choreographed by David Neumann. Producers are Amanda Lipitz, Henry Tisch and Jordan Roth. title: David Ayer to Become a Partner at Ryan Kavanaugh’s New Location-Defying AI Company (Exclusive)
full_text: × Continue to The Hollywood Reporter SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All November 17, 2026 8:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source David Ayer attends the 'Heart of the Beast' photocall at the San Sebastian International Film Festival on September 23, 2026. Ayer is joining ACME AI, whose "Grey Box" aims to reduce the need for physical locations. Carlos Alvarez/Getty Images for Paramount Pictures He may have headed into the rugged with Heart of the Beast , but David Ayer says he may now have a new and more technological solution to shooting in the wilderness: AI . The director is joining ACME AI as a principal and managing partner, and will be involved in the operations of the firm. Founded by former Relativity Media co-founder Ryan Kavanaugh , ACME and its “Grey Box” tech allows directors and actors to shoot full-fledged scenes in far-flung locales without going anywhere. “When I got in there and saw what the tech can do I felt like a cowboy coming in off the range and seeing the first automobile,” Ayer tells The Hollywood Reporter . “I thought ‘I better learn how to drive this car or I’m going to be out a of a job.’” The Model T in question is known as performance transfer, and essentially it keeps above-the-line work intact while radically reducing the need for, and expense of, much of the below-the-line kind. ACME is part of a new wave of filmmaker-centric companies — they also include Jon Erwin’s Innovative Dreams and Matt Stone and Trey Parker’s Deep Voodoo — that allow for actors to perform dynamically in front of real-looking backdrops without ever leaving a soundstage. Romantic shots in the foreground of the Eiffel Tower? Check. Chase scenes through the streets of Tokyo? Why not? Essentially performance transfer functions as a digital green screen, but for everything. Proponents say the technique preserves all the physical aspects of a performance (and actors’ jobs) at far lower cost to a studio or the climate; think of it as Zoom work for thespians. Critics, however, say it risks losing the magic and serendipity of physical locations and hurts the livelihoods of on-set workers besides. (Department heads such as production designers and lighting artists would in many cases still be used, but in a more supervisory/advisory way than on a physical set.) Ayer says the chance to bring productions in at a much lower budget and nab greenlights that would otherwise prove out of reach makes it worth the tradeoff. “As a storyteller half my job is litigating over budget,” he says. “This pulls so many stories within striking distance.” ACME believes that, without the need to pack up and travel to a particular piece of geography and then set up shoots there, its tech can lead to a reduction in time and money at a rate of between 50 and 75 percent. To create the tech, ACME mapped many lenses and lighting packages to allow for a greater photorealism, and combined it with models that allow for the re-creation of the physical world. ACME’s Grey Box currently exists in Los Angeles on a dedicated stage, but the system could theoretically be replicated in other locations. (The company will rent the tech out to studios the way many soundstages currently do.) Doug Liman recently completed shooting the origins-of-crypto drama Bitcoin starring Casey Affleck using ACME’s Grey Box. The movie explores the mysterious origins of the title currency’s pseudonymous founder Satoshi Nakamoto without, for the most part, leaving the stage despite the Australian and other global settings. The idea of making big-budget-looking movies possible at mid-budget prices could, if successful, prompt a host of downstream questions. Will audiences stop valuing (and paying for) high-octane spectacle in the same way given how much easier it will be to produce? Will a whole system of crews and physical locations be displaced? Will studio executives eventually put pressure even on mid-budget projects to lower their costs given the expectation of cheaper methods? And who, besides Christopher Nolan and Tom Cruise, will actually be allowed to shoot in intensive physical locations for months at a time? A former Navy enlistee, Ayer has had an eventful Hollywood trajectory. After an early career writing or directing acclaimed law-and-order-themed dramas ( Training Day , End of Watch) he entered the DCEU with 2016’s controversial Suicide Squad (on which he famously had a very different cut ). He has entered a new act with a spate of successes in the past few years, including the Jason Statham action film The Beekeeper and this fall’s dog survival thriller Beast s tarring Brad Pitt. It garnered strong reviews and became a solid worldwide hit . Ayer says he has at multiple projects in development that can be redirected to the Grey Box. He believes many entities in the creative ecosystem will benefit from such a re-channeling, including actors and directors. “The staging starts to feel more like a Broadway play, where you know exactly what you’re going to get,” he says. “If I’m not worried about getting kicked off a location or a lightning storm shutting me down, it takes away a lot of the friction of filmmaking and just lets me focus on the fine craft of directing.” THR

title: DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn & Peter Safran Out, Former Marvel Exec Jeremy Latcham In
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Re-Release With New Rosario Dawson Night Nurse Footage Sets Release ‘The ‘Burbs’ Actor Kapil Talwalkar Signs With Innovative Artists Entertainment Martin Sheen, Alexis Bledel, Clive Standen & Tate Donovan Set For Sports Drama ‘Raising Cole’ View All November 9, 2026 9:16am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Story Arc James Gunn and Peter-Safran; Jeremy Latcham Getty/John Winters In a seismic executive shuffle unlike anything Bruce Wayne could pull off at Wayne Enterprises, James Gunn and Peter Safran are leaving their posts as co-CEOs and Chairmen of DC Studios , jobs which they’ve held for the past four years. The dynamic duo will continue to produce on various DC projects and are returning to their full-time creative work. They’re currently in post on the Superman sequel, Man of Tomorrow which will open in theaters on July 9, 2027. Related Stories Executives Departing DC Co-Head James Gunn Reflects On “Trying” Four Years, Juggling Being Filmmaker & Exec News Skydance Floats First Earnings Report As Hollywood Mega-Studio: Sizing Up The New Empire Taking over the comic book entertainment label as President and Chief Creative Officer is former Marvel SVP of Production and Development, Jeremy Latcham . He starts in the position on Dec. 1 and reports to Skydance Motion Picture Group co-chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein. Note the tweak here in the reporting structure of DC: Initially the DC Bosses reported straight into the CEO (previously Zaslav, post-merger David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz). Now DC — like the other Warner film labels — reports into Goldberg and Greenstein. Latcham worked with Gunn previously on Guardians of the Galaxy. Latcham shepherded such mega MCU franchises as Iron Man, Guardians of the Galaxy, Spider-Man and The Avengers . He will lead DC’s film, television and animation slate, overseeing the creative pipeline, along with production, talent and strategy. Watch on Deadline

title: Departing DC Co-Head James Gunn Reflects On "Trying" Four Years, Juggling Being Filmmaker & Exec
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Justin Kroll Justin Kroll Film Editor @krolljvar More Stories By Justin The James Bond Search Shows How Daunting The Process Is In An Age When Everyone On Social Media Is An Expert Aaron Pierre And ‘Sisu’ Director Jalmari Helander Team on Action Thriller ‘Fairytale In New York’ From Netflix And Lionsgate Margot Robbie & Kristoffer Borgli Team On ‘The Week Of Pain’ From A24 And Square Peg View All November 9, 2026 11:33am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Story Arc James Gunn Theo Wargo / Getty Images Following the news that he and Peter Safran would no longer be co-running DC Studios in the wake of the Skydance-Warner Bros. merger, James Gunn has spoken out about his time at the studio. In the lengthy statement, which Gunn dropped on his social media platforms, he shares how proud he is of his four years at DC Studios, lists some of all the projects he oversaw during that period while also touching on his partnership with Safran, whom he described as “the smartest most competent person” he’s know. Gunn also admits that the four years atop DC Studios were “trying” and that he had grown to “dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job.” Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Chris Pratt "Would Love" If James Gunn Made Another 'Guardians of the Galaxy' After DC Exit News DC Studios To-Do List: Here's What Incoming Boss Jeremy Latcham Will Sort Through From The Gunn-Safran Era The statement comes after Skydance chose to replace Gunn and Safran with veteran exec Latcham as the president and chief creative officer of DC Studios. Gunn and Safran will continue to produce on various DC projects and returning to their full-time creative work. They’re currently in post on the Superman sequel, Man of Tomorrow which will open in theaters on July 9, 2027. You can read Gunn’s statement in full below: “Oh, boy. What a four years.” “Thanks to all of you who have supported me and Peter in our time as the heads of DC Studios. When I was a kid growing up in Manchester, Missouri, I used to write and draw my own comics with a mix of DC Comics characters and my own characters. Having full access to these characters to do whatever we wanted has been a dream come true. I didn’t know if I wanted this job when it was offered to me, but I just couldn’t pass up the unique opportunity. I’m glad I took the job.” “There have been so many highs along the way – releasing Superman and Clayface , making Peacemaker , reading the scripts to The People Vs , the entire process of Man of Tomorrow, which thus far has been the best filmmaking experience of my life, and numerous other moments.” “The highest of the highs have been all the talented and wonderful people I’ve worked with and grown to love: the DC Studios crew, our talented collaborators, our casts and crews, and the boisterous and hilarious fans. And the best part of all has been working with Peter Safran , the smartest and most competent person I know. You’ve been the best partner a person could ask for, and, more so, a truly good friend.” “But what only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least. I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years (Jenn, I love you and I’m sorry and you don’t need to feel guilty for being the happiest of all people that I’m no longer doing this job). And the thing my ADHD hyperfocus has had the most difficulty with has been dividing my time between projects I’m incredibly passionate about and the ones I’m not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head.” So, yes, I will miss the people around me, and I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I’m also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking. That’s not to say Peter and I are immediately done with DC or superheroes. We have Man of Tomorrow out this summer. And we’ve just been engaged on another DC project which I’m writing, and we’ll see where it goes after that. And, of course, the characters we set up will live on. Thank you so very, very much for embracing the characters and stories we’ve put on screen.
